articles.title: Omar said she will have to move due to threats following federal raid
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) said she will have to move out of her apartment in Washington, D.C., because of threats she’s received after federal agents execute...
articles.body:
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) said she will have to move out of her apartment in Washington, D.C., because of threats she's received after federal agents executed a search warrant at her residence last week as part of an immigration fraud probe .

"Obviously, I can't continue to live there … Because our address has been public and with the death threats that I deal with, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids visiting off and on, having people track them," she told MS NOW's Chris Hayes in a Wednesday interview.

The congresswoman, who also has a residence in her home state of Minnesota, told Hayes she woke up at 6 a.m. on Oct. 12 to learn federal agents had "surrounded her house" in D.C. She said the agents provided her a search warrant before going "room by room" and seizing 17 items, including her phone and other electronics.

President Trump and his administration have claimed that Omar's father lied about her age when she obtained U.S. citizenship in 2000 after their family emigrated from Somalia.

The Democratic lawmaker has denied these allegations and accused the Trump administration of waging a "campaign of political intimidation" against her in a social media post following the raid.

"If you had so confidently said I've committed a crime, why are you not saying in the beginning … we're going to subpoena people, we're going to do a grand jury, we're going to try to find evidence that would lead to an indictment? It's just it's all bizarre," Omar said in the Wednesday interview.

Last week, The Washington Post reported that federal officials under the first Trump administration reviewed Omar's immigration records in 2019 but did not find evidence of fraud.

The president has for years attacked Omar in social media posts and speeches for her political views and background. During comments to reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday, Trump slammed Omar as a "sick, very dishonest person … who hates our country."

"I hope they treat her fairly, but she's a very dishonest person," he added.

The Minnesota progressive said she has received an outpouring of support from her Democratic colleagues. She also responded to former President Obama's statement condemning the Trump administration's investigation into her as "appalling."

"I think a lot of the conspiracy world that I find myself in is the conspiracy world that was created around him, and so while some people might feel reserved in some of the information that they hear from these people, I think he is acutely capable of seeing what this is," she said.

Omar told MS NOW on Wednesday she feels "confident" that she has done nothing wrong.

"I am a person of enormous faith," she said. "And I know that … if I continue to live my truth, if I continue to fight for the right things, if I continue to stand up to bullies and people who are carrying out ungodly corruption, I'm going to be OK."

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers’ second debate clash sets up final sprint in Michigan
articles.summary: The second Michigan Senate debate Wednesday featured several heated clashes between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former Rep.
articles.body: The second Michigan Senate debate Wednesday featured several heated clashes between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, though it was far tamer than an explosive first meeting this month. The debate took place in Detroit less than two weeks before Election Day in the bitterly contested battle for an open Senate seat. Polls show a neck-and-neck contest to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat. El-Sayed sought to tie Rogers to President Donald Trump at every turn and painted his opponent as a corporate sellout. Asked about addressing cost-of-living concerns, El-Sayed said rising gas and grocery prices are products of the war with Iran. “We need a war powers resolution rather than a senator who is going to stand hip to hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now,” El-Sayed said. “I’m looking forward to standing with my colleagues in the United States Senate to hold Donald Trump accountable for this war. The other thing that we’re going to need to do is take on the corporations who bought and sold politicians for a very long time.” Rogers has sought to create space with Trump on the war in recent weeks. He cut an ad calling for the war to wind down, though he has also said there was good reason for Trump to go to war initially to target Iran’s nuclear program. In an interview with NBC News last week, Rogers said, “I don’t think so,” when he was asked whether Trump made a mistake launching the war. Separately, Rogers aimed to tie El-Sayed to Islamic fundamentalist groups overseas while questioning his résumé and trustworthiness. “Everything that he said is not accurate, not correct,” Rogers said in response to criticisms from El-Sayed, adding that El-Sayed had misled voters about his connections to the Muslim Brotherhood and his own medical background. “This is a pattern that we need to understand for us to trust this candidate.” Rogers has sought to elevate the Muslim Brotherhood in the final weeks of the race, claiming on several occasions that El-Sayed and his family had connections to the Islamist organization. On Wednesday, he said El-Sayed asked the leader of the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt “to defund the police there, too. I mean, it’s unbelievable.” El-Sayed responded, “He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I’ve never been a part of because of my mom, who’s a nurse in Missouri.” In their last debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed’s mother, Fatten Elkomy, over her work at a charity the U.S. government later labeled a supporter of terrorist groups, leading to its closure. Elkomy was never accused of wrongdoing. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied any connections to the Muslim Brotherhood, telling NBC News last week, “I have no ties, we have no ties,” when he was asked about the accusations. “It doesn’t make any sense, and it’s actually really quite beneath you, Mike. It’s really quite beneath you,” El-Sayed said Wednesday. “To call into question my loyalty to the Constitution.” The exchange culminated in the most heated moment of the debate as Rogers tried to interrupt El-Sayed. “I’m talking,” El-Sayed said, pointing his finger at Rogers. “I am talking. I’m talking. Excuse me.” “To bring into question my commitment to the Constitution is really beneath you. I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American,” El-Sayed continued. “I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray, and the question that you would ask that, I think, is actually really quite shameful.” Rogers responded that El-Sayed “could pray any way you want, and I know you want to make this about you being a victim,” adding, “This is about an ideology.” The debate highlighted a contrast in style between the two candidates that has been playing out for months on the campaign trail, though El-Sayed was far less aggressive than he was during the first contest. El-Sayed looked directly into the camera nearly the entire time he was speaking. Rogers, meanwhile, offered few looks directly into the lens, opting instead to make eye contact with the moderators. The moderators kept tight control over the candidates’ time to answer questions and appeared to get through every subject they wanted to address, with the debate concluding a couple of minutes before the full hour had passed. They addressed healthcare, immigration, crime, Social Security and tariffs, among other issues. On tariffs, Rogers seemed to put additional distance between himself and Trump after he called this month for an end to the trade war with Canada. He said Wednesday that although some tariffs had brought “positive” developments for the state, “maybe these Canadian tariffs were not well thought-through.” He framed himself as someone who could stop Trump from enacting policies that would harm Michigan. “You might want to send the guy back who can actually get the meeting to get these things worked out,” he said. “If it’s good for Michigan, I’m going to be for it. If it’s bad for Michigan, I’m going to be against it.” Later, El-Sayed questioned the idea of electing a Republican senator to best rein in Trump. “So I’m just trying to figure out how this is going to go,” he said. “Donald Trump’s going to help him get into the United States Senate, and he’s going to turn around and stand up to Trump? Because, you know, we’ve got a real history of Republican senators standing up to Donald Trump right now. I don’t see it happening.” Throughout the debate, El-Sayed referred to a “MAGA bingo” game for supporters to play at home as they watched the debate, with the spots on the board being filled in by certain references from Rogers. Rogers retorted at one point that “the bingo game ought to be how many times can he put the word ‘Trump’ in any answer.” “Any answer that he has given in the last, whatever, 30 minutes?” Rogers said. “It’s ridiculous. This is really about the best way forward for Michigan.” The candidates also laid out their visions on artificial intelligence. Rogers said he supports an antitrust exemption for the frontier AI companies that covers only coordination on the safety of their technology, and he suggested he might be in favor of a so-called kill switch for programs that become dangerous. El-Sayed, who recently released an updated AI platform, said that he wants a pause on frontier research and that lawmakers must address “the fact that even the CEOs of these corporations think they could take 50% of the white-collar jobs over the next five to 10 years.” “So we need to make sure that we have AI under democracy, meaning that there’s going to be democratically appointed folks on the boards of these AI corporations,” he said. “There also should be AI no-gos. AI should not be able to fire you, shouldn’t be able to fire a weapon, shouldn’t be able to deny you health insurance.” The candidates also answered a series of rapid-fire questions at the end of the debate. On expanding the Supreme Court, El-Sayed said he was in favor of doing it, “but fairly.” Asked whether he supported universal background checks to purchase firearms, Rogers said it “depends.” After El-Sayed and the moderators said it was a yes-or-no question, Rogers said he was “in the middle.”

articles.title: Wisconsin governor candidates tangle over the economy, Trump and the 2020 election in tense debate
articles.summary: Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany faced off Wednesday night in the only debate in the race to succeed Gov. Tony Evers in the perennial battleground.
articles.body: Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany sparred Wednesday night in their sole debate in Wisconsin’s race for governor, sniping at each other on affordability, President Donald Trump, abortion and the 2020 election. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, and Tiffany, a member of Congress representing a northern Wisconsin district, are in a close race to succeed retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers — the first open governor’s race in the state since 2010. The debate most prominently focused on economic issues, with each candidate taking aim at the other over whose policies would best bring down prices. Tiffany vowed to undo various tax increases and return surplus dollars to residents, while Crowley advocated for a “fair tax system” that would fund education, infrastructure and transportation. Throughout Wednesday’s hourlong debate, Crowley frequently linked Tiffany to Trump and his policies — including the “big, beautiful bill,” tariffs and the war with Iran — that he said have raised prices in the state and nationally. He also accused Tiffany of “doing the bidding” of “the billionaire class,” pointing to the donations he has received from Republican megadonors. “When Congressman Tom Tiffany says he’s focusing on affordability, let’s be very clear: He voted for the big, ugly bill that [helped] some of the highest earners here in the state of Wisconsin,” Crowley said, referring to the 2025 tax cut and spending bill that reduced funding for healthcare and food assistance programs in many states. “We don’t need what is happening in Washington, D.C., coming into the state of Wisconsin. It is very clear that he is working for Donald Trump and the billionaires who are funding his campaign,” Crowley added. Tiffany retorted that “while my opponent” was “consistently focused on being against Donald Trump, I’m for Wisconsin — and rather than creating a bunch more programs that are going to end up taxing the people of Wisconsin more, I want to put more money in the taxpayers’ pockets.” Later, he accused Crowley of sounding “like a socialist.” Following a competitive primary this summer in which he beat state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, by fewer than 4,000 votes, Crowley had sought to downplay the policy differences between them as part of an effort to unite Democrats. “I think it’s really important to know that he said there’s very little difference between me and Francesca Hong,” Tiffany said of his opponent Wednesday night. “That sounds like a socialist to me.” Later in the debate, Tiffany was pressed about his votes to overturn the 2020 presidential election results as a member of Congress. Responding to questions from the moderators, Tiffany said, “One of the reasons that I did that is Zuckerbucks.” After the 2020 election, Trump allies falsely claimed that the millions of dollars Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg donated to groups helping election administration offices was a front by Zuckerberg to help Joe Biden win the election. Wisconsin voters banned the use of private funds in election administration by ballot measure in 2024. “Let’s be very clear — the congressman just said that the only reason why he was willing to throw away hundreds of thousands of votes here in the state of Wisconsin is because he disagreed on how somebody spent money,” Crowley said. “He has shown us that because of one disagreement, he’ll throw [votes] out,” Crowley added. Abortion also emerged as a contentious topic. Tiffany said he would uphold the state law allowing abortion access through 20 weeks of pregnancy. But in the House, Tiffany has supported so-called heartbeat bills that would ban abortion care at about six weeks of pregnancy. He said Wednesday that he would not sign legislation that would restrict abortion access at six weeks. Crowley has said that as governor he would work with the Legislature to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution. He reiterated that plan Wednesday and declined to say whether he’d sign a bill that would legalize abortion with no gestational limits. “I don’t believe a law like that would ever actually reach my desk,” he said.

articles.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar details federal search of her D.C. home, says she’ll have to move for safety reasons
articles.summary: The Minnesota Democrat said her husband and son were home when federal agents began banging on her house doors at 6 a.m. before they conducted an hourslong search.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Wednesday described in detail for the first time the early-morning search of her home last week by federal agents, revealing in the process that she can no longer live there because of safety concerns. In an interview with MS NOW, Omar said she and her husband were initially startled and confused by the arrival of agents with Homeland Security Investigations, who began banging on their doors and yelling at 6 a.m. Oct. 12. “Well, I mean, you don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you were trying to freak them out, and, you know, it obviously did freak all of us out,” Omar said. Federal agents searched Omar’s home as part of a criminal investigation that has alarmed Justice Department veterans who cited its proximity to the midterm elections. A person familiar with the investigation has told NBC News that the possible charges against Omar include conspiracy and making false statements in immigration paperwork. Omar told MS NOW she had “only had 2½ hours of sleep” when the agents arrived since she had returned home from a trip in the early morning. “It was, you know, trying to figure out, like you’re dreaming, this weird thing that’s happening,” Omar said. “But they basically, like, surrounded the house. They were pounding, pounding on the back door and the front door.” She said she and her husband yelled down to try to communicate that they were coming downstairs momentarily as they rushed to get dressed. Omar added that one of her three children, her 20-year-old son, was also at the residence. “I thought something was on fire. I thought something was happening to the neighbor,” Omar said, adding that she was particularly confused when she saw HSI agents at the door, since they often focus on issues like human trafficking, drugs, cybersecurity and terrorism. “The fact that they were at my house that early in the morning, you know, was so, so bizarre,” she said. “I was like, ‘Why are you here?’” Omar said the agents presented her with a warrant at the door after she asked to see one. They then asked her to sign a paper that would waive certain rights she has as a member of Congress, Omar said, adding that she declined to sign it. Under the Speech or Debate Clause of the Constitution, members of Congress are protected from civil and criminal liability relating to their legislative acts. Omar said in the interview that the agents took 17 items from her home, including old phones belonging to her and one of her daughters. Seizing the phone of a sitting member of Congress typically triggers a set of law enforcement protocols to ensure the Speech or Debate Clause is upheld. The search took “four or five hours,” Omar told MS NOW. “I don’t think I was able to call my attorney until about an hour into the search,” she said. Asked what she was doing during that time, she said, “I sat on the couch, staring at the warrant, trying to make sure that they were staying within the bounds of what the warrant allowed them to do.” The Department of Homeland Security referred NBC News to the Justice Department, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Omar’s account of the search. In addition to the phones, Omar said, agents took multiple items belonging to her husband, Tim Mynett, including a camera that was passed down by his uncle, a Somali phrase book that he was using to learn the language and his notebooks. Omar said that according to the receipt she was given after the search, she does not believe the agents took anything with her DNA. She also said she was not asked to provide a DNA sample. Overall, Omar said, the agents “mostly conducted themselves in a decent way.” “They did a really good job in putting everything back in its place,” Omar said. “They actually even folded some of my clothing that were not folded.” Still, Omar criticized the federal investigation. “The people who knocked on my door, searching for papers, literally have his papers,” Omar said, referring to the paperwork filed by her late father. “They are the ones who processed us to come to the United States.” She said that after the search, she can no longer live at her Washington home. “Obviously, I can’t continue to live there, because our address has been public,” Omar said. “And with the death threats that I deal with, it’s not, it’s no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids, like, visiting off and on having people track them.” Omar rejected President Donald Trump’s insistence that he had “nothing to do” with the investigation. “I mean, he’s got everything to do with it,” she said. “You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported.” Omar has been a frequent target of Trump since his first term. He has called her “garbage,” accused her of fraud and called for her deportation. Omar said she feels “confident in my truth” as she again denied the allegations against her. “How more obvious could these people be? You know, it’s, like, you could at least have the appearance of not having this be fictitious,” Omar said. “But they’ve chosen to blatantly have every character that has been involved be someone who has expressed explicitly that they don’t want me to be in the United States.”

articles.title: Kansas Senate rivals distance themselves from party leaders in fiery debate
articles.summary: The Kansas Senate debate saw Roger Marshall and Adam Hamilton try to define each other by their parties as Senate control hangs in the balance.
articles.body: Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton repeatedly sought to distance themselves from the most unpopular elements of their respective parties Wednesday night during a contentious Kansas Senate debate. Both candidates battled over President Donald Trump, immigration, the war in Iran and more in a race that could help determine control of the Senate. The debate opened on a personal note, with both candidates pressed over controversies that have fueled attack ads in the closing weeks of the campaign. Marshall was questioned about a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. The Republican defended the practice while emphasizing the millions of dollars in free care his practice provided. GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS "Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall said. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric." Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp alleged to have been a sexual predator. Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp after an initial investigation. "I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part." The candidates spent much of the rest of the debate trying to define each other by their respective national parties. Marshall repeatedly warned that electing Hamilton would help hand control of the Senate to Democrats and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, while Hamilton sought to portray himself as an independent-minded Democrat willing to break with his party. THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND That divide came into focus when the moderator played footage of Trump campaigning for Marshall in Kansas earlier this week and telling voters to "pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot." Asked whether that meant he would support every part of Trump's agenda, Marshall said no and pointed to recent disagreements involving immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and beef imports. "Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right." Nevertheless, Marshall emphasized his support for much of Trump's agenda and urged the president's supporters to turn out for him. "We need the Trump voters to come out," Marshall said. "If you want the Trump agenda to continue, if you want secure borders, if you want a strong military, if you want lower taxes, then you â and you voted for President Trump â you need to come out." Hamilton faced a similar challenge when moderators pressed him over his past support for Democrats and his campaign message of "leading from the middle." MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN The Democratic nominee explicitly broke with former President Joe Biden over immigration. "The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton said. "I believe in strong and secure borders." Hamilton also said he would not support Schumer for majority leader if Democrats win control of the Senate. The debate did produce an unusual moment of agreement when both candidates were asked how many genders there are. "There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded. SC DEM SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS SHE WILL STAND UP TO HER PARTY AS GRAHAM TIES HER TO 'SOCIALIST DEMOCRATS' Hamilton later said he did not want biological males competing against his 12-year-old granddaughter in sports, calling it "not a fair fight," while arguing that decisions over athletic participation should generally be handled locally rather than by the federal government. The Kansas contest has emerged as an unexpectedly competitive Senate race in the closing weeks of the midterms. Marshall is seeking a second term in a state that has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, while Hamilton, a longtime pastor, has campaigned as a moderate Democrat. articles.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her Washington, DC, home after federal search
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid...
articles.body:
U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there.

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives , a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Wednesday in her first interview since the search that she is "confident in the fact that I didn't do anything wrong."

The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.

In the interview with MS NOW , Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.

Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items , including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children's book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.

The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation .

Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000.

"It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I'm sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seams like a leap," she said in the interview.

The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.

Omar said the agents were "intrusive but polite," logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.

Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

articles.title: Trump voters reveal their biggest fear heading into midterms — and it's not rising prices
articles.summary: Trump rallied supporters in Wichita as the Kansas Senate race between Roger Marshall and Adam Hamilton tightens to a dead heat in the polls.
articles.body: WICHITA, Kan. â Voters at President Donald Trump's Kansas rally said the cost of living remains a major concern, but many feared Democratic control of Congress even more. This midterm election cycle features six Republican-controlled Senate seats that are considered toss-ups, including Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall's contest against Democrat Adam Hamilton. That race has become an unexpected challenge for Republicans in their quest to keep control of the Senate. And voters who lined up to get a chance to see Trump in Wichita told Fox News Digital that they recognized the stakes, particularly the effect Democrats flipping both chambers of Congress could have on the president's agenda. SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS "Trump doesn't get the support that he needs to protect America, and that our country will turn into Paris, France," Kathy Bond told Fox News Digital of the riots roiling through the French capital. "That's my biggest concern." The race between Marshall and Hamilton, who led the Church of the Resurrection which now boasts a congregation of nearly 23,000, according to the church's website, before jumping into politics. The Cook Political Report recently shifted the race to a toss-up, sending Republicans scrambling to dump more money into the state. Trump's rally in Kansas, the first time a sitting president has visited the Wichita area since former President George W. Bush in 2007, is part of his and Republicans' broader strategy to motivate Republican voters during a midterm election cycle in which he is not on the ballot. National Republicans argue that without the loyal MAGA voting bloc, they wonât stand a chance as they face turbulent political headwinds. THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES Though voters are unhappy with the economy, the ones waiting in the long, snaking lines to get their seat inside the Heartland Credit Union Arena argued that Democratic control would be worse. "We've got to vote Republican down the ballot this year. It's a significant point in the Trump administration," Emily told Fox News Digital. "And it's just we've got to keep the Republican majority. There's too much at stake." Marshall, who is running for a second term in the upper chamber, recognized that the race was neck and neck and told Fox News Digital in an interview before the rally that "it's the price of gas" that has tightened the race. "I do feel people's pain," Marshall said. "Every year I go to all 105 counties, finish up the 105 counties in June, and as that price of gas went up, I felt more and more frustration. So maybe we're up 12 points before the Iran War, and as the price went up our poll numbers went down, so I think it's the price of gas." WOKE MEGACHURCH PASTOR, DEM NOMINEE CALLED FOR REPENTANCE OVER WHITE PRIVILEGE IN WAKE OF GEORGE FLOYD, BLM "But I think people are beginning to realize the rest of the story, that if we were to lose this seat and let Democrats control the Senate, they would go back to their policies that drove gas prices up higher," he continued. "Even today, the price of gas is less on average under President Trump than it was under Joe Biden." Some at the rally felt that Marshall should have to answer for his votes in the Senate but believed that his experience as a lawmaker overrode the uncertainty that the political newcomer Hamilton could bring should he win on Nov. 3. "But for me, somebody like Hamilton that hasn't been in, you know, this game and doesn't really know exactly what all this entails," she continued. articles.title: WATCH: Top 3 clashes in heated MN governor debate as Walz's legacy looms large: 'Change the culture'
articles.summary: Minnesota GOP House Speaker Lisa Demuth and Dem. Sen. Amy Klobuchar clashed on several issues in their final debate with Gov. Tim Walz being a focal point.
articles.body: The Republican and Democratic candidates vying to replace Minnesota's outgoing Gov. Tim Walz sparred in their final debate Wednesday over the massive fraud scandal that has unfolded in the state, healthcare and rising gas prices. MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL "A vote for Amy Klobuchar is a vote for a Tim Walz third term," Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth said in her opening statement after painting Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar as the "status quo" candidate in a "state in crisis" over the $9 billion fraud scandal. Klobuchar pushed back in her opening statement, saying, "I don't like the status quo. I hate the status quo." WALZ'S 'EXIT INTERVIEW' REFLECTING ON HIS TENURE SPARKS LAWMAKER DEBATE ABOUT HIS LEGACY: 'NEVER SERIOUS' The first question of the debate focused on fraud, a recurring topic throughout the night, and what each candidate would do to combat it. "Fraud unchecked here in the state of Minnesota has gone far too long, and it has finally come to the surface," Demuth said. "The thing that I will do on day one is I am going to be firing all commissioners, choosing new commissioners that are expert in their field that will carry out the accountability and transparency that is needed in our state. We have to change the culture of fraud." Klobuchar attempted to distance herself from Walz when addressing the issue. "The fraud is simply unacceptable and, as a former prosecutor, I'm going to send those fraudsters to jail," Klobuchar said. "Tim Walz should have caught the fraud earlier and he should have done more. He said it himself. And by the way, when my opponent references Tim Walz, I will say one thing. He is not seeking a third term. I am the one up here." Fraud came up again later in the debate, with Demuth criticizing Klobuchar's close relationship with Walz. "You have not heard my opponent differ from one policy bill that Tim Walz, who she calls an incredible governor, has allowed to go forward," Demuth said. "I would love to hear one bill, one area, childcare, fraudulent funding. I would love to hear that. If she is separating herself specifically from Tim Walz, Tim Walz allowed the childcare fraud and other fraud here in the state of Minnesota to explode to $9 billion, never firing any of his commissioners or agency employees. But yet you have someone standing here tonight that is supporting everything from the incredible governor, as she has said he is." Klobuchar responded, "Rewind the tape on this debate please; you will see exactly how I said I differed from Tim Walz." RISING GAS PRICES In another tense moment, the candidates turned to rising gas prices, with Klobuchar attempting to link Demuth to the policies of the Trump administration. "I can tell you the fastest way to bring down your gas prices, and that is to stop this War in Iran," Klobuchar said. "That is it, beginning, middle and end. And when you look at what my opponent brings up, when we had a debate earlier this week, she actually brought up and blamed it on the Keystone pipeline. Then she blamed the healthcare costs on Barack Obama. I don't know what will be next. Maybe Thomas Jefferson, but what I know is that Minnesotans understand what's happened at the pump." EXPLOSIVE SLEEPER ISSUE COULD FUEL MIDTERM SHAKEUPS, TOP REPUBLICAN PREDICTS: âYOUâRE GONNA SEE SURPRISESâ Demuth blamed high costs in Minnesota on the Minnesota DemocraticâFarmerâLabor Party's (DFL) control of state government. "We can talk about that Keystone pipeline that my opponent has voted against. That would have brought in 830,000 barrels of oil. It would have helped with the supply that we have here, yet she voted against it," Demuth said. "But you have to ask yourself, why are things so expensive here in Minnesota? They are expensive because of overspending by a one-party control in 2023 and 2024. I will bring down prices. I will right-size our state budget and make sure that you can afford your lives, that you can grow, thrive, and businesses will be coming to Minnesota to provide the jobs that are needed. It's common sense, and that's the decision that you have to make as you're looking to this election this year." HEALTHCARE COSTS AND INSULIN PRICES As Minnesotans continue to grapple with rising healthcare costs, the two candidates sparred over ObamaCare, which Klobuchar voted for in the U.S. Senate. "It's important to realize that we're looking at all of the inputs and all of the reasons why our healthcare is more expensive," Demuth said. "Senator Klobuchar supported the Affordable Care Act. She promised that it would bring down our healthcare. Unfortunately, we have seen anything but all of our healthcare since the Affordable Care Act has increased the healthcare cost to all Minnesotans." Klobuchar didn't address ObamaCare in her response, instead pointing to Demuth's position on abortion and accusing the Republican of being beholden to Big Pharma. "You've heard from my opponent that, I don't support certain things in healthcare, she's talking about issues that are already settled," Demuth said. "I think it's quite rich to hear the fact that she is the one that broke the healthcare system as the deciding vote on the Affordable Care Act." During the healthcare discussion, Klobuchar argued that Demuth has not done enough to lower insulin prices and cited the support she has received from the family of Alex Smith, a 26-year-old Minnesotan who died while struggling to afford his insulin treatments. "Just to clarify a very incorrect or untruthful lie that you just heard was the fact that I did vote yes for the Alex Smith insulin bill," Demuth responded. "Back in April of 2020. The governor signed it into law the very next day." Before serving in the Senate, Klobuchar was elected twice as county attorney in Hennepin County, Minnesota's most populous. She also ran unsuccessfully for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination. Demuth, who was first elected to the Minnesota House in 2018, has served as GOP leader in the chamber since the start of 2023 and as speaker for the past year and a half.

articles.title: Abortion, ICE and socialism spark fireworks in swing state governor debate: 5 top moments
articles.summary: Republican Tom Tiffany pointed to a 20-week abortion limit while Democrat David Crowley declined to name a gestational cutoff in their debate.
articles.body: Republican Tom Tiffany and Democrat David Crowley sparred over abortion, taxes, immigration and Wisconsin's growing data center industry Wednesday night as Wisconsin's gubernatorial candidates faced off in a heated debate. Tiffany, a Republican congressman, and Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, offered competing visions for Wisconsin as they vie to succeed Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. The WISN-hosted debate came less than two weeks before Election Day, with polls showing a tight race. A September Marquette Law School poll found Crowley leading Tiffany 49% to 46% among likely voters, a difference within the survey's margin of error. RealClearPolitics rates the race a toss-up. WISCONSIN GOP GOVERNOR CANDIDATE SWIMS FROM SINKING PLANE AFTER EMERGENCY LAKE LANDING Here are five of the biggest moments from the debate. 1. Tiffany points to 20-week abortion limit as Crowley declines to name one Tiffany pointed to Wisconsin's existing 20-week abortion limit when moderators asked whether he would sign a six-week abortion ban, a restriction he previously supported as a legislator. "I voted for a five-month bill when I was in the state Senate. I will uphold that law as the governor of the state of Wisconsin," Tiffany said. "I have been very clear where I stand. I've given the answer that I'm at five months," he added. Tiffany also sought to reassure women about his position. "All you women out there, you will not have to hold your breath when I'm governor," he said. Crowley, meanwhile, declined to specify a gestational limit for legal abortion, even when moderators asked whether he supported abortion through nine months. "These are discussions that need to be made between a doctor and a patient," Crowley said. âMODERATEâ DEM GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE EMBRACED DEI BUDGET TOOL, GREEN NEW DEAL-STYLE POLICIES Tiffany accused Crowley of supporting abortion through "the full nine months." Crowley countered that abortions later in pregnancy typically involve extreme circumstances and criticized Tiffany's previous support for stricter abortion legislation. "My position has been consistent ever since I announced for governor," Tiffany responded. "We once again did not hear where David Crowley stands on abortion." 2. Tiffany vows to return Wisconsin's entire $3 billion surplus The candidates split over Wisconsin's nearly $3 billion projected budget surplus, with Tiffany pledging to return the entire sum to taxpayers through permanent tax cuts. "We should return all of that to the taxpayers. They've overpaid into the state of Wisconsin," Tiffany said. Tiffany favored permanent tax cuts over rebate checks, arguing Wisconsinites cannot plan their finances around one-time payments. His proposal includes income and property tax reductions, including a 10% middle-income tax cut. Crowley argued the surplus should be used more broadly to lower costs for families, including through property tax relief and investments in public schools, municipalities, childcare and healthcare. Tiffany argued Wisconsin could cut taxes without sacrificing funding for education, transportation and healthcare. Crowley countered that Tiffany's plan would deprive state and local governments of revenue needed to provide those services. 3. Candidates draw stark battle lines over ICE Tiffany pledged to require Wisconsin sheriffs to honor federal immigration detainers, drawing a sharp contrast with Crowley over cooperation with ICE. "I will make sure that local, county and state law enforcement coordinate with federal law enforcement," Tiffany said, arguing immigrants who commit crimes should be transferred to federal authorities while still in county jails. Asked whether that cooperation should be mandated by law, Tiffany said, "I believe we should." Crowley opposed a blanket ban on cooperation with federal immigration authorities and said immigrants convicted of crimes should be deported. However, he called for restrictions on ICE operations in Wisconsin, including ending contracts with local law enforcement, prohibiting agents from wearing masks and requiring judicial warrants before entering jails and prisons. "We need to make sure that we're protecting people's civil liberties," Crowley said. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER 4. Data center boom puts subsidies, farmland and energy costs in spotlight Wisconsin's data center boom emerged as another campaign issue, with both candidates opposing taxpayer subsidies for the massive projects. Tiffany outlined conditions for data center development under his administration, including protections against higher utility rates, a ban on taxpayer subsidies, local control, farmland protections and greater transparency. "Why would some of the wealthiest companies in the world need subsidies from the taxpayers of Wisconsin?" Tiffany said. Crowley said communities should not be forced to accept data centers they do not want and said he would sign legislation eliminating sales tax incentives for the projects. Crowley also supported the current pause on data center development pending an environmental review and called for greater reliance on renewable energy to meet rising electricity demand. 5. Crowley says he's 'not familiar' with DSA platform Crowley faced questions about the Democratic Party's left flank after narrowly defeating democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the Democratic gubernatorial primary. Asked which democratic socialist priorities he shared, Crowley cited expanding BadgerCare, funding public education and childcare and holding wealthy Americans accountable. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But when moderators asked which parts of the Democratic Socialists of America platform he supported, Crowley said he could not answer. "I'm not familiar with the DSA platform to be answering that question," Crowley said. Tiffany pointed to Crowley's previous claim that little separated him from Hong during the Democratic primary. "That sounds like a socialist to me," Tiffany said.

articles.title: Independent voters aren’t picking a political team, they just feel picked on
articles.summary: Independents are now the largest bloc of American voters, and their views on immigration, energy costs and AI don't fit either party's platform.
articles.body: Regardless of the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections, any party that wins the majority will have done so because of the independent vote. For the past several elections, this cohort has been the crucial swing vote that ultimately decides the election. Independents are the kingmakers. If Democrats win big on Nov. 3, expect a familiar story. Pundits will call it a mandate. Party leaders will say voters want their agenda. They will be wrong. I have spent my career in partisan politics, and I keep seeing the same mistake. Both parties read the results of a protest as an endorsement. LEE CARTER: POLLS SAY DEMOCRATS COULD SWAMP REPUBLICANS. AS A POLLSTER, I HAVE A QUESTION Here is why. Independents do not fit neatly into a partisan box. They are not secret Democrats, and they are not secret Republicans. They agree with each side on some things and with neither on others, which is exactly why neither party can claim them. That does not mean they lack convictions. Independents, like most Americans, have coherent views on politics and policy. And these positions are widely shared and present opportunity for meaningful legislation. On energy, 70% of Americans want government to actively expand supply: more energy, lower prices, less pollution. On immigration, 77% want legal immigration maintained or expanded, focused on the skills the economy needs. Respect our laws and welcome those who contribute. WASHINGTON REWARDS FAILURE. ITâS TIME TO SEND CAREER POLITICIANS HOME On technology, 83% want parents to have the legal right to see and control what their kids do on social media. On spending, 73% want to bar Congress from using accounting tricks that hide the long-term cost of a bill. On corruption, 78% support term limits for members of Congress. A growing share of the country is independent, yet very few members of Congress are. That gap is the story behind the story this November. Put those together and the agenda is clear. Live within our means. Keep our promises. Win the future while protecting our communities, kids and liberties. Build a government accountable to people, not parties. That is not the progressive wish list, and it is not the Republican platform either. A vote against whoever is in charge is not a vote for anyoneâs program. It is a demand for these things. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AIâS PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS Look at what independents are actually upset about. The border is still unresolved after years of promises. Energy costs keep squeezing family budgets. And artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping jobs and daily life while Congress offers speeches instead of a plan. These are not left or right complaints. They are complaints about people in charge who are not getting results. Independents are now the largest bloc of American voters. They decide close elections, and they have no loyalty to either team. They vote for whoever seems least likely to make things worse. Two years ago, that was one party. This year it may be the other. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT The numbers tell the story. Roughly two-thirds of independents say Washington does not hear them. That is not a number that describes people who have found a new political home. It describes people who feel abandoned and are looking for the exit. For a blue wave to occur, it will rest on independents who are holding their noses. They will be voting for Democrats because the alternative looks worse, not because they have embraced the progressive wish list. Treating that vote as a blank check is how a party loses the same voters two years later. MINNEAPOLIS PROGRESSIVES TURN ON GEORGE FLOYD-ERA PUBLIC SAFETY OVERHAUL, PUSH TO DISMANTLE OFFICE Consider crime. Most Americans, whatever their party, want safe streets and a justice system that works. Imagine House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries stepping to the microphone to announce a serious, commonsense crime bill. Fund good policing. Go after repeat violent offenders. Protect due process. It would not be a radical idea. It would be a reasonable one. Win the future while protecting our communities, kids and liberties. Build a government accountable to people, not parties. That is not the progressive wish list, and it is not the Republican platform either. That single act would change the national story. Independents would take notice. It would say the party is willing to govern from the center and listen to people who do not agree with it on everything. SCANDALS, SOCIALISTS AND TRUMP ROIL PRIMARIES, SEND INCUMBENTS PACKING AT NEAR-RECORD PACE But that bill will not come, and the reason is not hard to see. A party that wants the support of the middle is being pulled by a left flank that treats a compromise on public safety as betrayal. Groups like the Democratic Socialists of America hold enormous sway over the energy and the primaries. Jeffries cannot move toward the center without a fight inside his own coalition, and so he does not try. That is the real danger for Democrats. The very independents who may hand them a majority will be watching to see what they do with it. If the answer is a sharp turn toward the activist left, those voters will leave just as fast as they arrived. NEWT GINGRICH: REPUBLICANS CAN WIN THE 2026 MIDTERMS â IF THEY FOLLOW THE PLAN Republicans should not take comfort either. If they lose, it will be because they too failed to listen. Both parties have spent years competing for the loyal base and ignoring everyone else. The result is a country in which most voters feel they are choosing between two disappointments. There is a better path, and it is not complicated. Secure the border and fix the legal immigration system. Lower energy costs by building what we need. Set sensible guardrails on AI before the technology outruns us. Do these things in a way that respects voters of every stripe, and independents will reward you. Ignore them, and they will punish you, whatever letter follows your name. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION This is why just a few handfuls of independents can entirely change the way we view and conduct politics. A growing share of the country is independent, yet very few members of Congress are. That gap is the story behind the story this November. The honest answer will decide whether this election is a turning point or just another swing of the pendulum. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM ADAM BRANDON

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: Trump must go to war on the airwaves to stop Democrats’ blue-wave blitz
articles.summary: Trump should deliver a primetime address warning voters that a Democratic blue wave would paralyze his agenda on Iran, spending, and the Supreme Court.
articles.body: Should President Donald Trump deliver a primetime address next week with the avowed purpose of impacting the elections nationwide? Yes. Absolutely yes. President Trump is often the best proponent of his own policies, and the much-anticipated "blue wave" would effectively paralyze those policies and his plans to finish the battle with Iran, build the Golden Dome and Golden Fleet, and slow, if not reverse, the regulatory overhaul underway. MORNING GLORY: MINNESOTA'S MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL COULD DELIVER A STUNNING SENATE UPSET Loss of the Senate majority would also mean near-zero chances of confirming any appellate judges or Supreme Court justices. Spending on the Pentagon would also plummet as Democrats return to their long-standing position of insisting that every dollar of increased defense spending must be matched by one for non-defense domestic discretionary spending. If President Trump makes these arguments directly to voters and names the names of the senators or Senate candidates who are key allies or the Democratic nominees he believes are from the far, far left, the sharpened focus could help mobilize his base to again support his agenda one last time. 13 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS, TRUMP HEADS TO SOUTH CAROLINA AS DEMOCRATS WIDEN BATTLEGROUND MAP There are precedents for such an appeal, and they had mixed results. On October 24, 2022, President Biden made a direct closing argument for Democrats at Democratic National Committee headquarters, 15 days before Election Day. The expected "red wave" that year was reduced to a ripple. On October 25, 2006, President George W. Bush held a nationally televised news conference less than two weeks before the midterms. President Bush discussed Iraq and framed the election choice around national security and taxes. It was a news conference, not a formal primetime address. The GOP got "thumped," to borrow President Bushâs own characterization of the 2006 results. The takeaway from that limited data set? A speech could work to rally a presidentâs base voters. A press conference wonât. President Trumpâs rallies around the country have always served as a feedback loop for his messaging. He knows itâs his base that turns out, and he tries out various messages and themes, then amplifies what works and cuts what doesnât in subsequent rallies and in his conversations with the press. Getting the feedback is particularly important when it comes to turning out the base. As the president has been everywhere in the past month, he has a good idea of what "works" in this campaign cycle. TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG The Trump PAC may even want to buy network time for an address, or it may simply allow social media to do its thing. A tight 15 minutes would play and play, give birth to ten thousand posts and reels and, crucially, focus the base and independent voters on the stakes, which are very high indeed. President Trump has got a fine writing staff, but brevity is not second nature to him or them when it comes to speeches. If he does try such a direct appeal, the crucial points I hope he makes in succinct fashion are these: TRUMP'S UNUSUAL ROLE AT MIDTERM CONVENTION REVEALED AS SCHEDULE GOES PUBLIC VOTERS PREPARE TO WEIGH-IN ON TRUMP'S ECONOMY AS COSTS CONTINUE TO SURGE The president should explicitly ask voters to support Mike Rogers in Michigan, Michele Tafoya in Minnesota, Ken Paxton in Texas and Susan Collins in Maine. President Trump should note that Rogers and Tafoya are likely to be as independent-minded as Sen. Collins, who has often opposed presidential policies, but that all of them represent their states very well. States that are "light blue" or "light red" deserve senators that represent them, not Hamas or other extremist positions. President Trump should close by reminding everyone of the mess he inherited. The once wide-open border is now completely closed and sealed tight, with the long-awaited wall nearing completion. Fraud in Minnesota, California and other blue states is being exposed and corrected. Inflation is way down from the 9.1% it reached under President Joe Biden but needs to go down further still, and President Trump and his economic team can get that done with support from Congress, not obstruction. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION And the evil regime in Iran that has terrorized the world for 47 years is on its last legs and wobbling. Its nuclear weapons program is obliterated and will not be allowed to be rebuilt. There is work to be done with our allies across the globe, but taking us down the impeachment road because the Democrats have no proposals to do anything else would be a disaster for everyone. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Americaâs Golden Age is indeed upon us," President Trump should conclude. "I need your vote, and so do these great Republican candidates. Please make a plan to vote and turn out. Thank you. God bless our troops everywhere, but especially in the blockade and at the bases around the Islamic radicals in Iran, and those confronting Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis, and God bless the United States." A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman Universityâs Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. articles.title: El-Sayed’s alleged ties to Muslim Brotherhood shake up Michigan Senate race
articles.summary: Senate Republicans are making a last-ditch effort to save former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the Michigan Senate race by pouring money and effort into highlighting what they say are significant ties between Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed vigorously denies that he has any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans are making a last-ditch effort to save former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in the Michigan Senate race by pouring money and effort into highlighting what they say are significant ties between Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood.

El-Sayed vigorously denies that he has any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group that is viewed as an influential predecessor to some prominent fundamentalist Islamic groups. Congress has investigated the Muslim Brotherhood as a potential global threat.

But the issue is not so simple, as Republicans have dug up past statements by El-Sayed they say are sympathetic to the Islamist movement that briefly took over Egypt in 2012 and 2013.

In an essay published on HuffPost in January 2011, El-Sayed argued that if the Muslim Brotherhood were to take power in Egypt after the overthrow of Hosni Mubarak, the result wouldn’t be as bad as some critics feared.

He argued the military wouldn’t back the group’s leadership bid unless “strong liberal democratic structures were in place” and dismissed comparisons warning the Muslim Brotherhood taking control of Egypt would be akin to Hamas’s leadership in Gaza.

Republicans are also pointing to a statement El-Sayed signed in 2012 after Islamist leader Mohamed Morsi gained power in Egypt, urging him “to purge the media and police as quickly as possible.”

“We affirm, as Egyptian Americans, that we strongly reject those voices that are courting America and Europe to take a position against the Egyptian regime,” the letter’s signatories declared.

His support for the letter was first reported last month by The Washington Free Beacon.

El-Sayed has now been thrust into the awkward position of having to defend years-old social media posts from his half-sister claiming their family has long had ties to “MB,” referring to the Muslim Brotherhood. She also said that some relatives had been jailed in Egypt because of activism in the group.

The candidate’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, revealed on social media in 2012 that she had an “amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.”

Her mother, Fatten Elkomy, is El-Sayed’s biological mother.

El-Sayed’s parents immigrated to the United States from Egypt but divorced when he was only 3 years old. He was then raised by his father, Mohamed El-Sayed, and stepmother, Jacqueline Johnson, outside of Detroit.

Even so, Republicans are going all in on trying to portray El-Sayed as radical, playing off some of his more controversial statements during the Democratic primary, such as calling Israel a “rogue state” and endorsing “Medicare for all.”

Rogers confronted El-Sayed over the allegations at their second debate Wednesday evening.

“Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” he demanded of his opponent.

It was a more effective stab at the topic than at their first encounter on the debate stage, when El-Sayed was able to shut down a line of attack aimed at his birth mother’s political affiliations.

Rogers also sought to divide Democratic voters by appealing to “Jewish Democrats who are afraid for their children,” playing on the Republican effort to frame El-Sayed as allied with Islamic fundamentalists and the pro-Palestinian movement.

El-Sayed sought to rise above the attacks by declaring “I love this country” and “I love the Constitution.”

Political experts say Republicans may be trying to play on some voters’ apprehensions about electing the first Muslim member to the United States Senate.

“It may be the Muslim Brotherhood is radical, which of course it was,” said Ross K. Baker, a professor of political science at Rutgers University, who noted the group hasn’t figured very prominently in news from the Middle East recently.

“The name, Muslim Brotherhood, suggests something sinister, and I think that’s probably why they’re using it,” he noted.

President Trump has declared El-Sayed is “100 percent” affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood, and other prominent Republicans, such as Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), are piling on.

Cruz has challenged whether El-Sayed, if he wins the Michigan race, should have access to sensitive national security information in Congress as a potential member of the Senate Armed Services or Intelligence committees.

“There would be an unacceptably high risk that American servicemen and women, their lives would be in danger, and that our covert intelligence assets, their lives would be in danger, because there’s every reason to believe that Abdul El-Sayed would share that information with Muslim Brotherhood terrorists,” Cruz declared Tuesday during an interview with Fox News’s Sean Hannity.

El-Sayed over the weekend disavowed any loyalty to the Muslim Brotherhood when asked about it during a town hall.

He followed that up by telling Newsmax in a brief interview at a public event that he “clearly disavowed” the group and bristled at any implication that he would harbor a dual loyalty with the fundamental Islamists.

“The implication of the question is that somehow I have dual loyalties, right? And there’s nothing about my history or record to imply that,” El-Sayed said.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to The Hill’s requests for comment.

Two Republican super PACs backing Rogers are now spending big on ads tagging El-Sayed as tied to the fundamentalist Islamic political group.

A Senate GOP strategist keeping tabs on the Michigan race said that Great Lakes Conservative Fund and Senate Leadership Fund, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), appear to be spending millions of dollars on ads attacking El-Sayed over his family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and his past statements that appear sympathetic to the group.

“I think it’s affecting the race. I think it’s hurting El-Sayed,” the source said. “The ads are on pretty frequently, and I do think it’s made the race turn.”

“There’s one from the Great Lakes Conservative Fund that deals with it pretty directly, and there’s another Senate Leadership Fund [ad] that deals with it,” the strategist reported.

The spot by the Great Lakes Conservative Fund highlights El-Sayed’s efforts to distance himself from the Muslim Brotherhood, including an appearance on NBC News’s “Meet the Press” when he categorically denied any ties.

The Great Lakes Conservative Fund contrasts El-Sayed’s claim to NBC host Kristen Welker that neither he nor his family has any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood with multiple past social media posts from his half-sister that appear to call his answers into question.

The ad also highlights video footage of El-Sayed telling an audience that “Muslims definitely hate you” and another clip where the candidate acknowledges he has dual U.S.-Egyptian citizenship.

John Clark, a professor of political science at Western Michigan University, said El-Sayed’s alleged ties or alleged sympathies with the Muslim Brotherhood are becoming a high-profile issue in the Senate race because of the barrage of Republican spending.

“Certainly, it has a lot of visibility, at least in the media I’m consuming. It’s everywhere. There’s so much money coming in,” he said. “The advertising windows are just filled with ads for the Senate race.”

“The Senate ads and these allegations are really all over the place,” he added.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) is leaning in hard on the alleged ties between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood.

“Abdul El-Sayed and his family’s ties to designated terrorist groups have raised so many red flags that even the mainstream media can no longer ignore them. El-Sayed has serious questions to answer, and it should alarm every single Michigander that he continually refuses to do so,” said NRSC regional press secretary Samantha Cantrell.

Clark, the political scientist from Western Michigan University, said some voters are likely to be turned off from El-Sayed when they hear about his alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood but questioned whether it would ultimately make much of a difference in the race.

“I think [it] has become the perceived way to make an impact,” he said of the Republican strategy. “Certainly for folks who have been paying attention to Abdul El-Sayed at least through this campaign, if not before, this is not going to affect them very much at all.”

“People voted for him knowing this would likely be a topic during the general election campaign,” Clark continued. “I have yet to see anybody that I consider to be credible that can make these direct ties that [Republicans] are claiming.

“The [half-] sister who was from a later marriage of the mother says she had a conversation with her mother about her connections to the Muslim Brotherhood in the 1970s; I’m not sure it really carries much water with folks,” he said.

“Here’s where the impact is: The idea of a Muslim anything scares the hell out of a lot of people and so that’s what the Republicans are going for,” he noted. “In that sense, it might make in a big difference.”

articles.title: Khanna to introduce bill that would establish Truth and Accountability Commission
articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is introducing legislation that would create the first-ever Truth and Accountability Commission to investigate what he calls abuses of power by the Trump administration. The bill, first shared with The Hill, notes the commission would examine several issues, including the administration’s decision to launch a war in Iran without congressional authorization.…
articles.body:
Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is introducing legislation that would create the first-ever Truth and Accountability Commission to investigate what he calls abuses of power by the Trump administration.

The bill, first shared with The Hill, notes the commission would examine several issues, including the administration’s decision to launch a war in Iran without congressional authorization.

It would also examine President Trump and his family’s alleged use of public office for private enrichment; unreleased files related to deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein; “shootings and other uses of force” by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol officers; and other executive branch actions, such as the firing of federal employees under the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and funding freezes.

Khanna, who has not ruled out a 2028 presidential bid, told The Hill that Americans across the country are demanding accountability from the Trump administration.

“I completely disagree with Democrats who say that we should not impeach Trump. I completely disagree with Democrats who say, ‘Let’s just have a kumbaya moment and move on.’ I am the wing of the Democratic Party that is going to demand accountability and demand the investigation and prosecution for anyone who broke the law,” Khanna said.

The commission would consist of 11 members, with the chairperson selected by the president. The minority and majority leaders in the House and Senate will each select two members to serve on the commission. The remaining members will be appointed by the chairperson from a list of no less than five individuals submitted by state attorneys general affiliated with the Republican and Democratic Parties.

Asked whether he thinks Republicans will be supportive of the effort, Khanna said, “I believe that once they lose in the midterms, people are going to start to break with Donald Trump.”

“They’re going to recognize that they don’t want to hang their political future on a corrupt administration, and I will work as I did with [Rep. Thomas] Massie [(R-Ky.)] on accountability on these issues. I mean, standing against corruption is something that is going to be bipartisan,” the congressman said.

Khanna partnered with Massie in authoring and pushing for the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which Trump signed into law last year. Khanna has also pushed for the prosecution of individuals tied to Epstein’s sexual abuse and exploitation.

If Democrats win back the House majority in November, their investigations, legislative priorities and oversight of the Trump administration could serve as both a test of their ability to govern and a blueprint for the party’s broader political message heading into the 2028 presidential race.

Khanna said he believes this commission “can set the standard in 2028 for what the Democratic base and what voters expect of the next president.”

“They expect a president that’s going to hold the elites accountable. They expect us to not just move on, but to make sure that we have the rule of law followed. They expect us to hold Trump’s family accountable, Trump’s administration accountable, the people who committed illegal acts accountable, and have the courage and the strength to stand up for that, instead of just saying, ‘Okay, we’re going to move on and let’s pretend this never happened,’” Khanna said.

articles.title: A new socialist bloc could test Jeffries from Day 1
articles.summary: Democratic socialists have already made huge waves this cycle by knocking off a handful of House incumbents on their way to Washington. The big question now gripping the party is how disruptive they’ll be when they get here. “We don’t know how they will be part of the team,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) said. “We…
articles.body:
Democratic socialists have already made huge waves this cycle by knocking off a handful of House incumbents on their way to Washington. The big question now gripping the party is how disruptive they’ll be when they get here.

“We don’t know how they will be part of the team,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) said. “We hope they’ll be part of the team, but we don’t know.”

The answer to that question could play an outsized role not only in steering the Democrats’ legislative agenda in the next Congress, when they’re favored to control the lower chamber, but also in molding the party’s image heading into the 2028 elections, when they’re hoping to seize the White House after four years under Trump.

A handful of incoming liberals backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are vowing to press Democratic leaders to champion far-left policies — like “Medicare for All” and cutting aid to Israel. Some are already calling for the president’s impeachment.

They’ve hammered their own party for what they see as an abandonment of progressive ideals and a soft-glove approach to President Trump’s second term.

That agenda could create headaches for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), who’s in line to become Speaker if the House flips, and present difficult votes for centrist front-runners who are crucial to winning and retaining a Democratic majority. The wildcard remains, however, how much sway the DSA bloc will have — and how hard it intends to push in demanding action on its liberal wish list.

Heading into the elections, the Democratic anxieties about what might happen when the democratic socialists arrive are already bubbling up.

“The main question is: What is it like when we have these people here? Do they try to create problems?” said one House aide. “Do they say stuff that all our members get asked about? … We’re not super enthusiastic about [that].”

Democratic socialists are nothing new to Capitol Hill. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) have carried that torch in the Capitol for years. But the stunning victory by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani last year has given the movement a new shot in the arm, and his endorsement of several DSA House candidates helped propel them to victory in primaries earlier this year.

The DSA candidates hail from all corners of the country, including Michigan, where state Rep. Donavan McKinney defeated Rep. Shri Thanedar; Colorado, where Melat Kiros bumped off Rep. Dianna DeGette; and New York, where Darializa Avila Chevalier toppled Rep. Adriano Espaillat and Rep. Dan Goldman was ousted by former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander, a former DSA member.

What unites them is a belief that Democrats on Capitol Hill haven’t fought hard enough for their traditional values and interests.

Still, even within the DSA there are conflicting sentiments about how hard the incoming socialists should push Jeffries and his leadership team. On one side of that debate are the progressives, who see their remarkable success in the primary elections as an opportunity to shake up Washington — even if it means battling their own party brass.

“There’s no time like the present,” said one DSA member, who requested anonymity to discuss a sensitive topic. “This is our year, and we’ve gotten the attention we need thus far. It would be foolish to let go once we actually get to Capitol Hill. Voters are asking for change, that’s the biggest takeaway of this cycle. They want changes in how we govern and how we do business.”

At the same time, a second DSA member predicted there wouldn’t be much bomb-throwing from that flank of the party.

“I don’t want DSA to become a party of no,” the member said. “It does get you gains in the short term, but it’s not a governing strategy.”

Nomiki Konst, a progressive strategist who is an inactive member of the DSA, predicted that most of the left in the caucus are going to side with Jeffries. She pointed to the contentious early days of Ocasio-Cortez, another democratic socialist who was first elected in 2018, and her struggles to push then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

Now, Konst said, the new DSA congressional members “have learned the lessons” of Ocasio-Cortez.

Still, she added, “You have a runway in the beginning and you should absolutely put some pressure on him [Jeffries] to be on certain committees and push on popular issues like Medicare for All.”

Whatever the case, the incoming democratic socialists are sure to create challenges for Jeffries and other Democratic leaders, who will face the tricky task of balancing the competing interests of an ideologically diverse party.

On one hand, Jeffries will want to cater to base voters with bold legislation expanding healthcare benefits, strengthening environmental protections and reining in Trump’s deportation machine. On the other hand, leadership will have to tread carefully to ensure that those proposals don’t tip so far to the left that they harm the chances of centrist Democrats in battleground districts, where the House majority is won and lost.

“The first priority for House Democrats when they get the majority will be to unify around a strategy to keep it. That means focusing on consensus that reflects Democratic vision and values while also protecting members facing tough reelections in purple districts,” said former Rep. Steve Israel (N.Y.), who once led the House Democrats’ campaign arm.

“Building that unity won’t be easy, but I think Hakeem Jeffries is made for this moment,” he added. “He’s kept everyone together in the minority and he has the skill and leadership to do it in the majority.”

How the saga plays out will likely depend heavily on how many seats Democrats pick up in the midterms. If there’s a huge blue wave, then Jeffries and other party leaders will have a comfortable cushion to pursue their agenda without much fear that it will be derailed by defections from either end of the spectrum, socialists or centrists. Smaller gains, however, would leave party leaders with little wiggle room when they bring bills to the floor, lending much greater power to small blocs of lawmakers to demand action on their priorities.

Jeffries has largely held Democrats together under Trump’s second term, but there have been cracks in the armor, including two high-profile episodes in September when a pair of centrist Democrats hopped the aisle to advance the Republicans’ agenda, infuriating much of the party.

Beyer, the Virginia Democrat, said those defections could forecast trouble with the DSA lawmakers coming in next year — but the margins will be crucial.

“If we get 230 or 232 or something, much less so,” he said. “But if it’s 220?”

Those dynamics will get an early test run in the first week of January, when Jeffries will be seeking the Speaker’s gavel, and the DSA members — most of whom have not committed to supporting Jeffries — will have to decide how hard to flex their muscles. Again, the size of the Democratic majority could play a major factor.

“If we’re at 218, 219, 2020, then Jeffries would really have to buckle down,” said the House aide, “because every single person can throw him out of it just by being a no.”
