articles.title: Trump, Republicans spend big in midterm home stretch
articles.summary: Republicans are banking on last minute injections of cash to boost the party’s most vulnerable candidates less than two weeks out from Election Day. President Trump announced on Tuesday that his political operation will spend over $400 million to support GOP candidates, while the Republican National Committee (RNC) confirmed it is transferring $50 million…
articles.body:
Republicans are banking on last minute injections of cash to boost the party’s most vulnerable candidates less than two weeks out from Election Day.

President Trump announced on Tuesday that his political operation will spend over $400 million to support GOP candidates, while the Republican National Committee (RNC) confirmed it is transferring $50 million into groups behind the efforts to defend the House and Senate majorities.

The massive spending effort comes as polls show the Republican majority in an increasingly precarious position.

“I’d rather have it in a toss-up situation than not, but at this point, it’s going to take more than money in either direction, Republican or Democrat, in some of these contested races to get through the finish line and get there first, but money is a part of that equation,” said one Republican strategist, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

According to recent Federal Election Commission filings, the president’s MAGA Inc. super PAC has spent $277 million over the last six weeks.

The RNC moved over $44 million to the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) and the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) from mid-August to mid-October. The two committees evenly split the funds. Both committees are also expected to receive $6 million more from the RNC before Election Day.

Some Republicans have said they would have liked to see more spending from groups like MAGA Inc. sooner, noting that rates for advertising space spike before elections.

“It’s certainly better than nothing but it is still [two times] if not more the cost of a candidate ad,” the unnamed strategist said.

The RNC’s infusion to the NRCC and NRSC is aided by a summer Supreme Court ruling that walked back restrictions on political party spending, allowing parties to coordinate and spend unlimited sums with campaigns.

“We’re now deploying it aggressively and strategically to directly benefit our candidates when and where it has the highest impact, giving Republicans the hard dollar edge in key battleground races across the country,” RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said in a statement announcing the transfer on Tuesday.

Republicans are spending big as they appear on track to lose the House, with just a 22 percent probability of holding the majority in the latest forecasts from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Their chances are better in the Senate, but there’s a 56 percent probability the upper chamber could also slip away.

Cook Political Report on Tuesday shifted its ratings of 11 House districts and two Senate contests away from the GOP, while they moved just one Senate race away from Democrats.

“Even a novice political observer would have told you a month ago Republicans were going to lose the House,” said the unnamed Republican strategist

Observers say another sign that the House majority is a lost cause comes from Trump’s blitz through red states to prop up candidates in key Senate races and play defense in districts long seen as lock-ups for the party.

Along the trail, Trump has urged his base to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and pledged $5,000 “Trump dividends” for U.S. adults if Republicans keep control of both chambers.

He said on Tuesday that he’s already spent over $300 million on “Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity and more” in the midterms, with plans to spend upwards of $400 million by Election Day.

The closing-weeks cash surge could certainly help, said a second Republican strategist, but with just two weeks to go until the election, “money has diminishing returns right now” amid a “supersaturation rate” for ads.

“Most of the TV has been purchased. There’s always options for digital, but a ground game, some sort of a get-up-a-vote effort, which would turn out low propensity voters, would be key or ideal, but we’re just so late in the game,” the strategist said.

That’s forcing campaign operatives to make strategic decisions as races come down to the wire.

Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst for DDHQ, pointed to recent reports that Republicans are pulling money out of some tough races, including cuts in battleground House districts in New Jersey and Iowa.

Such moves could be interpreted as Republicans “almost admitting that they’re going to lose the House,” Skelley said.

“The challenge with the sort of ad spending and outside spending data is that, especially this late in the ball game, that dollar is not going nearly as far in terms of booking ad time,” Skelley added. “And we have continued to see Democratic candidates raising a lot more money than Republican candidates. … At the same time, look, Republicans definitely have more money.”

The RNC entered the year with a staggering $100 million cash advantage over its Democratic counterpart, but Democratic candidates pulled in massive third-quarter sums , according to the latest filings.

From July through September alone, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico raked in $64 million in his Texas race against Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton, while Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) brought in $33 million against Trump-backed Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.). Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed also notched $31 million against former Rep. Mike Rogers, another Trump pick, in Michigan.

“You’re trying to defend the Senate, and well, you’ve got really expensive TV markets in Texas, and you’ve got millions and millions and millions of dollars that you can throw at the problem,” Skelley said of Republicans and the congressional map. “It’s like, well, of course you’re going to throw the millions. Whether or not it can work to substantively change the race is harder to say.”

articles.title: Talarico, Paxton in dead heat for Texas Senate, Abbott leads governor’s race: Poll
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are in a dead heat for the Senate in Texas, according to new polling of one of the cycle’s most closely watched contests. Talarico notched 48 percent to Paxton’s 46 percent in new numbers from Emerson College Polling and The Hill, a result within the poll’s margin of…
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are in a dead heat for the Senate in Texas, according to new polling of one of the cycle’s most closely watched contests.

Talarico notched 48 percent to Paxton’s 46 percent in new numbers from Emerson College Polling and The Hill, a result within the poll’s margin of error. Another 5 percent were undecided, and 1 percent picked Libertarian Ted Brown.

When undecided voters were asked which candidate they lean toward, Talarico’s support jumped to 49 percent, Paxton to 48 percent and Brown to 3 percent.

“Since August, Talarico’s support has slowly inched up by about a point each month, from 46% to 48%, while Paxton has hovered between 46% and 47%,” said Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling.

Brown’s Libertarian bid could also change the game .

“If the Libertarian candidate, who is at 3% on the final ballot, sees his support melt between now and Election Day, Paxton likely sees his vote share increase as these third-party voters are independents or Republicans, but if it holds, Talarico benefits,” Kimball said.

Talarico and Paxton are locked in a tough race that’s drawn huge fundraising numbers and national attention in the tussle for Senate control. Republicans have long dominated the Lone Star State, but Paxton’s controversy-laden campaign and Talarico’s grassroots energy have given Democrats hope of their first flip in decades.

Talarico raised a staggering $64 million in the third quarter of the year, compared to Paxton’s $18 million . But tech mogul Elon Musk poured $158 million into a super PAC backing Paxton, according to filings last week, as Republicans try to keep the seat.

Meanwhile, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) boasted a slight lead in the Emerson polling of the gubernatorial race as he tries for a fourth term.

Abbott scored 49 percent to Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s 45 percent, while Libertarian Pat Dixon snagged 1 percent and another 4 percent were undecided.

When undecided voters were forced to a choice, Abbott jumped to 51 percent, Hinojosa to 47 percent and Dixon to 2 percent.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) rates the Texas Senate a toss-up, with Talarico narrowly favored. The governor’s race has a “lean Republican” rating, a step short of being a toss-up.

The Emerson College Polling Texas survey was conducted Oct. 17-19 among 1,000 likely Texas voters and has a credibility interval, similar to a poll’s margin of error, of plus or minus 3.1 percent.

articles.title: Fake polls fooled the political world. Now the midterms face a trust crisis
articles.summary: The political polling industry is under new fire after a second company on Tuesday acknowledged it had falsified data in a series of polls released over the past year. The admission by Wedgewood Polls comes as Republicans question whether this year’s midterm polls are wrong and are undercounting GOP support. Wedgewood’s polling had been used by…
articles.body:
The political polling industry is under new fire after a second company on Tuesday acknowledged it had falsified data in a series of polls released over the past year.

The admission by Wedgewood Polls comes as Republicans question whether this year’s midterm polls are wrong and are undercounting GOP support.

Wedgewood’s polling had been used by a number of media firms, including The Hill, The New York Times and The Hill’s polling partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

DDHQ and other aggregators quickly removed the fake results from their averages, but the incident is adding more uncertainty to an industry already dealing with issues with public trust.

“This is a new threat to polling,” said G. Elliott Morris, the founder of the polling aggregation and political analysis site FiftyPlusOne. “The story of polling methodologically is one of constant innovation. Now we’re in the environment where I think the people consuming polls will have to have to innovate as well.”

The disclosure from Wedgewood on Tuesday evening that most of its results were fabricated sent ripples throughout the polling industry and among political observers.

Wedgewood said in a statement posted on the social platform X that its endeavor was an “experiment” designed to test if a fake polling firm could gain traction and be taken seriously without much scrutiny in political discourse.

“Wedgewood Polling was never intended to sway an election or permanently mislead the public; it was designed as a wake-up call,” the post reads. “If a fictional entity run by a small group of industry veterans can be integrated into major polling averages and cited by major news organizations, the standards for how polling data is vetted, aggregated, and reported must change.”

But critics are pointing to real-world consequences of the fake results, which covered a wide range of Senate races from Michigan to Maine.

One such poll from Wedgewood released in June of the Michigan Democratic primary showed Abdul El-Sayed leading with 46 percent, followed by Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) with 39 percent. It was among a few early polls to show state Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D) bottoming out in the race, only receiving 9 percent support.

Following a few other polls that showed McMorrow well behind, she dropped out of the race.

McMorrow pointed to the poll result as a major factor in her donations drying up, and calls for her to exit the race.

Jennifer Holdsworth, who ran a super PAC supporting McMorrow, said in a post on X that the result was used by several donors as reason to pull back funding at a time when McMorrow supporters were being significantly outspent.

Several of Wedgewood’s fake results seemed to have at least somewhat favored Democrats. They generally weren’t total outliers compared to the findings of legitimate pollsters but added to a narrative of Democrats being in a strong position.

One showed Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson leading Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) by 4 points. Another showed El-Sayed leading former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in a general election poll by 6 points , more than most other pollsters have found.

In another fake result that if true would have been eye-opening, Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) only led Democrat Scott Colom by 4 points — a race deemed a significant longshot for Democrats even if a blue wave is on the horizon.

This isn’t the first time this year that fake results have been put out that received widespread attention. Another fake firm called Median Strategies disclosed in August that it put out two poll results, in the Wisconsin Democratic Senate primary and the Los Angeles mayor’s race, that were falsified.

The source of those polls was identified by The Guardian as Rahil Prakash, a 21-year-old recent college graduate who similarly told the outlet he wanted to put out the fake polling as part of a social experiment.

Who exactly is behind the Wedgewood results is unclear.

Efforts from The Hill to reach Wedgewood for additional comment were unsuccessful. An email to the address listed on its X account bounced back as undelivered, and its website is no longer operational. Its X account also requires a code to be input to message them on the platform.

Although Wedgewood announced itself that its polls were faked, an investigation from Morris’s FiftyPlusOne seems to have prompted the disclosure.

Morris and others who work at the site said in a blog post that they received an anonymous tip last week with evidence suggesting Wedgewood might be faking its data. After running an investigation and preparing an article exposing Wedgewood, FiftyPlusOne reached out for comment.

Wedgewood then went forward with its statement and messaged FiftyPlusOne to say “f— you,” the post states.

Morris told The Hill that this compounds the issue of declining public trust already facing legitimate pollsters who are genuinely trying their best to produce accurate results.

This incident came at a time when Republicans have been casting doubts on the polls as they have mostly shown Democrats poised for major gains on Election Day. They were quick to seize on Wedgewood’s disclosure that polling can’t be trusted.

“Left-wing outlets are just as culpable for platforming fake polls as the Democratic operatives who fabricated them. Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson may have fooled the press during their primaries, but their radical, tax-hiking agendas won’t fool voters this November,” said Bernadette Breslin, the national press secretary for Senate Republicans’ campaign arm.

Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr put out a post on X warning journalists and broadcasters against “amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics.” He said there has been a “significant surge in entirely fake polls.”

“The FCC takes these issues seriously. Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes,” he said.

Morris and other experts said this creates a distorted picture when the overwhelming majority of poll results have been legitimate. They reiterated that methods exist to try to decipher what can be trusted and what should be viewed with greater skepticism.

Ben Leff, the CEO and co-founder of the polling firm Verasight, noted that the American Association for Public Opinion Research (AAPOR) maintains accreditation standards for pollsters who meet minimum standards on key aspects of their process, including a clear and transparent methodology statement explaining how they gathered their data.

“You wouldn’t go to a doctor who wasn’t licensed or a lawyer who didn’t pass the bar, and media organizations should hold pollsters to the same standard,” he said.

Leff said checking if a pollster has the AAPOR certification is a good first step.

Still, the difficulty remains that even a methodology statement can be fabricated, as happened in the case of Wedgewood.

“I’ll be honest. Unfortunately, at some point, you can’t catch everything, right?” said Zach Donnini, the head of data science for the polling aggregator VoteHub. “Just because at any moment, someone can just decide to burn your reputation and start releasing fake polls, potentially even for nefarious financial initiatives.”

Donnini had been in touch with Wedgewood as well to try to probe their legitimacy. He said the difficulty was that Wedgewood had names tied to it who formerly worked for SoCal Strategies, which is a legitimate polling firm.

“It’s not like this is random people from nowhere. They actually conducted real polls before,” he said.

Leff said explaining that the fake polls are not at all connected to the polling industry is critical but may be difficult.

“Where the public is going to have to be really careful is on social media and online, because news networks are only a small portion of what people consume, and so it is going to be on the public to look at when they read results online that reference polls and making sure those seem like legitimate entities.”

articles.title: El-Sayed, Rogers clash over Muslim Brotherhood, Trump and guns: 5 fiery debate moments
articles.summary: Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed clashed over the Iran war, AI regulation, and the Second Amendment in a fiery Michigan Senate debate.
articles.body: Former Rep. Mike Rogers and his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, tore into each other at their second Michigan Senate debate Wednesday evening. Rogers, a former FBI special agent and the Republican U.S. Senate candidate, clashed with El-Sayed over the personal barbs, accusations and fierce divides that have defined one of the countryâs most anticipated Senate elections. Here are some of the most noteworthy moments from the fiery faceoff. El-Sayed accuses Rogers of backing Trumpâs war with Iran As evidence of Rogersâ alignment with President Donald Trump, El-Sayed accused him of backing the war in Iran, a conflict El-Sayed himself described as "aimless." "He's got a war for everything, and he won't back off the war now. He supports this war," El-Sayed said. "If you don't believe me, I want you to pay attention. On Sunday, when Donald Trump comes here at the invitation of Mike Rogers to remind you that, in fact, Donald Trump is on the ballot through Mike Rogers. They are hip to hip on this war, and you are paying the cost," he added, referring to one of Rogers' upcoming campaign events. Rogers quickly fired back, reiterating a moment from their first debate when El-Sayed refused to answer whether Israel or Iran posed a greater threat to the U.S. "My opponent can't even condemn the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps], which is the terrorist enforcement arm of Iran, and doesn't believe Iran is any more dangerous than Israel. This is an absolute nonstarter," Rogers said. THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS Rogers sparks explosive moment with resurfaced Muslim Brotherhood accusations At one point during the debate, Rogers accused El-Sayed of deleting social media content about defunding the police â a progressive stance that circulated among far-left Democrats in 2020 after the death of George Floyd. "I will tell you this: he did call for defunding the police â¦ [and] he deleted all of this material. Why would you do that? Why would you go through and take all of that time to delete all of the material? X videos, comments, podcast. Why? Because he was passionate about defunding the police," Rogers said. "As a matter of fact, he asked the Muslim Brotherhood head, Morsi, in Egypt to defund the police there, too," Rogers added, referring to the former Egyptian president associated with the group. The last remark triggered a fierce reaction from El-Sayed, who has fended off questions about ties to the Muslim Brotherhood throughout his campaign. "He keeps raising this question about this association with the organization," El-Sayed said. "It's really quite beneath you." Although Fox News Digital has not discovered any links between El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood, critics have pointed to El-Sayed's ties to the Muslim Students Association (MSA), a group listed as part of a strategy memorandum for North America written by one of the Muslim Brotherhoodâs members, Mohamed Akram. El-Sayed served as the vice president of the MSA chapter at the University of Michigan during his time there as a senior in 2007, according to College Fix. ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW Rogers blasts hidden costs of expanding government promises Throughout the night, El-Sayed doubled down on promises to expand government programs like Medicaid and measures to "put money in your pocket," a refrain that has been a cornerstone of his campaign. But Rogers made sure to cast doubt on those commitments, arguing that the policies would carry with them a heftier price tag than the Democratic nominee would acknowledge. "So think of all of the three things he just talked about. Put money in your pockets. It's a great slogan. There's nothing behind it. Matter of fact, when his Democratic socialist-aligned policies are engaged, you'll be lucky to have a d--- pair of pants when you're done," Rogers said. "Medicare for all. He doesn't tell you how much taxes you have to get charged, and you lose your private health insurance. These aren't real solutions. These are solutions that are going to make your life more miserable. And it's going to take away your choices in healthcare." Rogers claims El-Sayed said âquiet part out loudâ on AI regulation When asked about AI regulation, Abdul El-Sayed briefly mentioned he would support having "democratically appointed folks on the board of these AI corporations," citing what he described as an existential threat to the workforce. Rogers seized on the moment, accusing El-Sayed of verbalizing a desire to exercise public control of private companies. "He said the quiet part out loud," Rogers said. "He wants government to go into these businesses. That is the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). [They] come in for your business and your future. And so, you need to really stop for a minute and think about, do you want somebody who wants the government involved in these companies?" Rogers added. Notably, Abdul El-Sayed has not officially received an endorsement from the DSA, nor has he affirmed the groupâs platform. Even so, he has endorsed and received endorsements from a number of candidates who have received the DSAâs backing. Among them, El-Sayed supported New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a self-proclaimed socialist, in his bid for office last year. ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYEDâS âEXTREMEâ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION El-Sayed gets heat in rapid-fire round over Second Amendment At the close of the debate, Rogers fired back at El-Sayed when the Democratic candidate needled him for refusing to answer yes or no to a question about implementing universal background checks for gun purchases. "It all depends. It all depends," Rogers said. "Itâs not hard. Look at that. So dependable," El-Sayed quipped. Rogers fired back, noting that El-Sayed had once called for doing away with the Second Amendment in comments he had made before he launched his Senate bid. "You want to ban the Second Amendment. Why donât you talk about that?" Rogers was alluding to a video published on YouTube in 2023 in which El-Sayed had compared the right to bear arms to a right to healthcare. "What if we tweaked the Constitution, amended the amendment, and instead of the right to bear arms, we change it to the right to have healthcare?" El-Sayed said. He claimed altruism in the proposal, saying more people would live and arguing against individuals owning firearms, instead suggesting that only designated community-based groups like police forces should be issued firearms. The video has since been made private. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With their second debate now in the rearview mirror, El-Sayed and Rogers have closed out their scheduled debates and are unlikely to meet again until after the election. Having cleared their respective primaries and secured their parties' nominations, the pair will face off in Michiganâs general election on Nov. 3. After the debate, MIGOP Chairman Jim Runestad said in a statement to Fox News Digital: "Mike Rogers demonstrated yet again why he is the commonsense, steady hand Michiganders want to see in the U.S. Senate. We cannot afford Abdul El-Sayed's far-left, big-government policies, and we cannot risk electing a person who campaigns with the likes of Hasan Piker and seemingly justified the horrific terrorist attack targeting children and the Jewish community in Bloomfield Hills."

articles.title: France's riot chaos fuels Farage's warning that mass immigration failures could haunt another country next
articles.summary: Nigel Farage urged Americans not to repeat Europe's immigration mistakes, linking mass migration to France riots and widespread unrest on the continent.
articles.body: As violent riots grip France, British political leader Nigel Farage warned Americans against repeating what he described as Europe's mass immigration failures, arguing that years of unchecked migration have transformed European cities and fueled unrest that could eventually spread elsewhere. "People like me who were warning about this years ago have sadly been proven right, but the problems are gonna be here for a very, very long time," Farage told Fox News Digital in an interview. "Please, please don't make the same level of mistakes that we have," he said in his message to Americans. Violent riots have erupted across parts of Europe in recent weeks, particularly in France, with Farage pointing to years of mass migration and failed political leadership as key factors fueling the unrest. The Reform UK leader singled out Emmanuel Macron, arguing that the French president should have mobilized the military to confront the violence, after education protests spiraled into riots, destruction and theft. MACRON JETS OUT OF RIOT-TORN FRANCE FOR GULF TRIP AS POLITICAL PRESSURE MOUNTS "Macron was asleep at the wheel, and it isn't just that he was at a concert," Farage said. "And whilst the French do have effective police forces, the scale of the uprising, I mean the mass looting, the mass looting and violence that took place in Paris was genuinely horrendous." "Meloni's reaction was swifter and a better sign of leadership," Farage said, referring to the Italian leader deploying 500 military troops to Milan in response to recent riots. "But the problem is, for people like Macron, who have always said, any criticism of immigration, whether legal or illegal, makes you racist, they psychologically find it hard to face up to their own failures of policy." Farage warned that the unrest he described in France and elsewhere in Europe could eventually erupt in Britain, pointing to demonstrations in London and questioning whether British leaders would respond more forcefully than Macron. ITALY UNLEASHES MILITARY RESPONSE TO VIOLENT RIOTS AS FRANCE FACES A RECKONING OF ITS OWN "You know, my real worry is they can happen in this country too," Farage said. "We've got the same hard left here. We've the same hate mobs that march, chanting in the streets of London, from the river to the sea." "I'm concerned that these things could happen here. And I wonder whether a British prime minister has got any more courage than President Macron in France," he added. Farage contrasted Europe's failure to control its borders with President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown in the United States. TRUMP, WALTZ LINK FRANCE RIOTS TO MASS IMMIGRATION AS THOUSANDS ARE ARRESTED "Look, whatever you think of President Trump's current policies, one thing he has done, and he promised he'd do. He's closed the southern border," Farage said. Trump vowed Tuesday to treat potential rioters in the U.S. "very rough," pointing to the unrest in France, he said at a rally in Greenville, North Carolina, before being interrupted by a protestor in the crowd. "They're crazy, these people. Look at that guy. He's a nutjob," Trump said, in reference to the protester. He warned that he would crack down on potential threats, saying he would not allow similar unrest to take hold in the U.S. FRANCE COULD FACE EVEN WORSE DESTRUCTION WITH SECOND WEEKEND OF PLANNED RIOTS, STATE DEPT WARNS "That's what you witness over the last three or four days. You watch nutjobs like him in France ruining their country," Trump said. "We're not going to put up with it by the way." "If a possible threat, which could happen, I hope you won't get angry if I treat them very, very rough, because that's what's going to happen. They're not going to destroy our country," he said. On Tuesday, British counterterrorism police rearrested two men suspected of assisting Iranian intelligence in an alleged plot targeting RAF Fairford, a U.K. base used by U.S. bombers. Authorities say Iranian state involvement is "highly likely," though no charges have been filed. FOILED TERROR PLOT AT BOMBER BASE SIGNALS WIDER THREAT TO US MILITARY INSTALLATIONS: EXPERT Farage said he has foreshadowed such criminal acts, alleging that Iran has exploited illegal crossings of the English Channel to move operatives into Britain. "I've called again and again for this to be declared a national security emergency. I have been ignored. If the Americans removing their bombers from RAF Fairford isn't enough warning. I don't know what is," he said. articles.title: House Dem leader's attack on voter ID comes back to haunt him after election fraud bust in his home state
articles.summary: House Democrats' No. 3 leader, Pete Aguilar, faces GOP fire over opposing California's Proposition 39 voter ID ballot measure on Election Day.
articles.body: House Democrats' No. 3 leader is under fire for his opposition to voter ID in his home state of California. House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., spoke at a press conference earlier this month criticizing a measure on Californians' ballot this Election Day that, if passed, would mandate that voters show government-issued photo ID at the polls. He made the comments just weeks before the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a crime bust that saw several U.S. permanent residents accused of registering to vote despite not being citizens. MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., hammered Aguilar's opposition to voter ID and argued the DOJ's recent actions made it "obvious" that the ballot measure, called Proposition 39, was needed. "Give me a break," Calvert told Fox News Digital. "You have to show an ID to board an airplane, cash a paycheck, rent an apartment or even buy cold medicine at the grocery store. Democrats claiming that requiring photo ID before casting a ballot is somehow 'racist' or 'voter suppression' is complete nonsense and an insult to every voter's intelligence." NEW YORK CITYâS LONE REPUBLICAN IN CONGRESS ACCUSES MAMDANI, SCHUMER OF 'HYPOCRISY' IN VOTER ID FIGHT Rep. Vince Fong, R-Calif., said voter ID "is basic election security that the vast majority of Americans support, and 36 states already require." "While opponents are resorting to lies and fearmongering, Proposition 39 is commonsense reform in a world where you need an ID to rent a car, stay at a hotel, open a bank account or board a flight," Fong told Fox News Digital. "The DOJ's recent voter fraud bust in California is exactly why these safeguards matter." Rep. Young Kim, R-Calif., similarly said showing photo ID is a "simple standard we already require to board a plane, purchase alcohol or pick up a prescription." "This isn't controversial and it shouldn't be complicated. Our elections deserve at least as much consideration as a beer or a bottle of wine," Kim told Fox News Digital. Aguilar, meanwhile, criticized Proposition 39 during a press conference with Democratic gubernatorial candidate and former Biden administration Cabinet Secretary Xavier Becerra earlier this month. "We will not stand for this, because we will not stand for people to lose an opportunity to exercise their ability to vote. In Arizona, they tried this. They wanted folks to put their driver's license numbers on their ballots. Think about that. What if you miss one digit? Your vote doesn't count?" Aguilar proposed. "What if you're married in California? What if you're married, and you haven't changed your name and you go to vote? No longer will you be able to vote. That is what is at stake for Californians." SCHUMER SAID 'DEMOCRATS SUPPORT VOTER ID' â THEN EVERY SENATE DEMOCRAT VOTED AGAINST GOP BILL He called it a "voter suppression effort" pushed by Republicans. "Republicans can win only when they suppress the vote. Donald Trump and MAGA Republicans know that they are bankrupt of ideas and solutions, and so they have to change the rules of the game," Aguilar said. NEWSOM SPARS WITH TRUMP-APPOINTED PROSECUTOR OVER 20,000 SUSPECTED NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS Meanwhile, the California government criticized the DOJ's operation while pointing to reports that said more of those charged were registered as Republicans rather than Democrats. "For nearly a decade, Trump has baselessly alleged mass voter fraud rings were employed by Democrats and utilized 'illegal immigrants' to sway elections across the country â often pointing to California," a release on Gov. Gavin Newsom's state website read. "Courts at all levels have rejected the claims of vast voter fraud or that elections were rigged against the President." Voter ID laws currently exist in 36 states and polls have shown they have a majority of Americans' support. But in Congress, several efforts to pass federal voter ID legislation have been thwarted by Democrats in recent years. articles.title: Trump can’t deliver Ukraine to Putin — and he should stop trying to
articles.summary: Putin is losing ground. This is no time to reward him.
articles.body:
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Norway on Tuesday to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders. They brought the agenda: a one-sided peace deal with Russia, ending the war in Ukraine.

Nothing has changed since their last meeting in Kyiv . Russian President Vladimir Putin has not backed off his maximalist demands . Ukraine is not going to give up the remaining 11 percent of Donetsk , and the U.S. is not prepared to provide or support meaningful security guarantees.

Yes, President Trump wants an end to the war, but not for the sake of Ukraine or the defense of NATO; rather, to secure “ economic opportunities ” with Russia. Putin has had Kirill Dmitriev travel to Miami, Moscow, New York and Washington to entice Team Trump to win something that his military cannot deliver — Ukraine.

Trump has not been able to deliver Ukraine either. Mr. Art of the Deal cannot close the deal, and he continues using tactics unbecoming of any president before him to pressure Zelensky into making a bad deal.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth reportedly delayed the transfer of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles from European allies to Ukraine — missiles vital to Ukraine’s air defenses, protecting critical energy infrastructure and civilians from Russian missile attacks.

Ukraine’s access to Starshield was significantly degraded in mid-October, disrupting drone operations and battlefield communications. According to Reuters , the “order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House,” although Trump has denied any involvement .

Trump also continues to berate Zelensky publicly . As he departed the White House on Monday, he told reporters that Zelensky “doesn’t want to stop” the war and “is not helping matters much. I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”

Trump made no mention of Russian strikes against Ukrainian civilians or critical energy infrastructure. Only that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.” He has also made statements like, “Some people in a town that got hit or whatever , but mostly young soldiers.”

Images of dead Ukrainian children and their mothers tell a different story.

Trump said a couple weeks ago “that the war in Ukraine is drawing to a close ” and that “the end really is getting closer.” But that end cannot come at the cost of Ukraine. No business deal or economic opportunity is worth the cost of compromised American values — self determination, freedom, and democracy.

Yesterday, Trump told reporters, “ I want to see people not die . They’re losing, probably on average, 25,000 to 35,000 soldiers every single month. All I want is for Zelensky and Putin to stop the war.”

What he left out was that they — Russian soldiers — were dying only because they continue to attack Ukrainian defensive positions. They could leave at any time — Putin needs only to say the word. Ukraine, however, is facing an existential threat and defending itself. And it has become quite efficient in producing Russian casualties, surpassing 50,000 last month.

Putin’s army cannot win on the battlefield, but he is prepared to continue the Russian way of war until the West stops supporting his victim. He has mandated to the Kremlin a “ no-rules-now ” rule of engagement that essentially makes it open season on Ukrainian civilians.

But in reality, there have been no rules for the last four and a half years. And that is what we are witnessing today in Ukraine.

If Trump really wants to stop the killing, he should demand that Russian ground forces stop attacking, that the Kremlin stop bombing Ukrainian cities and that Putin withdraw his troops to within his country’s borders.

Team Trump is applying pressure to the wrong target. Putin has come back to the table out of weakness. Sanctions — the economic instrument of national power — and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have forced an unwilling Putin and Dmitriev back to the negotiating table. They need the economic investment to survive. This is no time to reward them for losing.

Putin’s economy and even his regime is in trouble. Ukraine has knocked out 51 percent of Russia’s oil refining capacity and has the other 49 percent on the target list as Fire Point missiles come on line.

Trump would give away the leverage that Ukrainians have died on the battlefield to create, in exchange for future economic opportunities Putin likely will not honor anyway.

Trump needs a new approach. He should exploit Putin’s weakness and flip the script. Peace must come at a cost for Moscow — not as a reward.

Any future deals with Russia must be contingent upon an immediate cease-fire, a Russian withdrawal from Ukraine and security guarantees. It must also include a cessation of Moscow’s hybrid war against NATO.

If Moscow refuses, economic sanctions must remain in place. And the U.S. must continue to provide Ukraine the intelligence support it needs to target Russia’s ability to fund and wage war, support a NATO active air defense over Ukraine and continue the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List program that provides Ukraine with weapons and ammunition.

Trump needs to be part of the solution and stop contributing to the problem Putin chose to create.

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: 4 key moments from debates in Michigan, Kansas, Wisconsin, Minnesota
articles.summary: In today’s issue: Candidates in some of the most critical Senate and governor’s races took to the stage for a final time Wednesday as voters have already started casting their ballots, with less than two weeks to go before Election Day. While President Trump is not on the ballot, he was at the center of the conversation…
articles.body:
Supreme Court blocks transgender prison policy

Witkoff’s ‘humanitarian’ comment faces backlash

Candidates in some of the most critical Senate and governor’s races took to the stage for a final time Wednesday as voters have already started casting their ballots, with less than two weeks to go before Election Day.

While President Trump is not on the ballot, he was at the center of the conversation Wednesday night, with Democrats seeking to tie their opponents to his most unpopular policies. Republicans sought to create some distance from the president, while casting their foes as extreme liberals aligned with the party’s far left.

Here’s four key moments as candidates made their final pitch to the voters.

As many Republicans are finding ways to distance themselves from the president as his approval rating has been plummeting, Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) took the opposite approach during Wednesday night’s debate against Democrat Adam Hamilton .

“If you want the Trump agenda to continue, if you want secure borders, if you want a strong military, if you want lower taxes, you voted for President Trump, you need to come out because we delivered on those things,” Marshall said, adding a vote for him is a vote for the president.

The debate was hosted by Nexstar Media Group, which also owns The Hill.

When pressed, Marshall noted he had criticized federal immigration operations in the state and Trump’s beef import plan.

“Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her,” Marshall said, adding that, while “my wife is always right, President Trump is not always right.”

Kansas voted for Trump by double digits in each of his elections. Hamilton also seemed to acknowledge that reality with his approach.

He emphasized that he’s not running against the president, only Marshall. He largely focused on attacking the incumbent and noted that some of his own supporters also back the president. Those are voters Hamilton will need if he is to pull off a win.

During the final Michigan Senate debate, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) plowed forward with his attack on Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with efforts to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood.

“Being bought off by the Muslim Brotherhood, having donors to his campaign from Hamas that support Hezbollah. It’s not a problem? If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers said.

El-Sayed hit back at Rogers for questioning his “loyalty.” Rogers has pointed to political contributions to El-Sayed from individuals with ties to the group, which Trump designated a terrorist organization last year.

“I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American,” El-Sayed said Wednesday. “I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray. And the question that you would ask that, I think, is actually really quite shameful.”

With Rogers trailing El Sayed in polls, Republicans are pouring money into the Muslim Brotherhood line of attack, The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports .

In the lone Wisconsin governor’s debate, both candidates had to walk a careful tightrope addressing touchy issues.

Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.) faced questions about why he voted against certifying the results of the 2020 presidential election. He initially avoided the question to shift the focus to his opponent, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (D), but eventually pointed to “Zuckerbucks” upon being pressed.

“We should not allow private money to go into what is a public process, our elections,” Tiffany said.

The term “Zuckerbucks” was coined by conservatives to refer to funds that the Center for Tech and Civic Life issued as grants for localities to facilitate the 2020 election during the COVID-19 pandemic. Most of the funding came from Mark Zuckerburg . Some alleged the funds were improperly used and benefitted Democrats.

Tiffany has stood by his vote against certifying the election in Pennsylvania and Arizona over the years, but the vote could come back to haunt him running statewide in a battleground state.

Crowley, meanwhile, kept his distance from his primary opponent, Francesca Hong , and other democratic socialists. He had said over the summer, as Hong was rising in the polls, that he didn’t differ with her on many issues. But took a different approach on the debate stage.

“I’m not familiar with the DSA platform to be answering that question,” he said about whether he supports the group’s priorities.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), who is running for governor, called the widespread fraud in the state’s social services programs in recent years “simply unacceptable” in her debate against state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R).

Klobuchar said Gov. Tim Walz (D), who was also former Vice President Harris ’s running mate in 2024, “should have done more” about fraud in the state, which has become a defining issue in the election.

Pressed on specifics by Demuth, Klobuchar said she would have caught the fraud sooner, used a $17.5 billion budget surplus more effectively, and would not have pardoned a Hmong man accused of sexually assaulting a child two decades ago. The man was deported by the Trump administration in July.

“You have not come up with one way you differ from Donald Trump,” Klobuchar said to Demuth.

Demuth later said she had broken with Trump on the Iran war and also criticized his trade war with Canada and a plan to import foreign beef.

“That’s the best you can come up with? I literally can’t believe it,” Klobuchar responded, saying Demuth waited too long to oppose the Iran war and bringing up deadly ICE sweeps earlier this year.

“You literally said Kristi Noem showed steady leadership when 3,000 ICE agents descended onto the streets of our state,” Klobuchar said.

▪ The Hill : El-Sayed, Rogers face off in final debate.

CRISIS OF CONFIDENCE : With the recent disclosure of more fake polls that fooled much of the political world, the polling industry is facing the seemingly Sisyphean challenge of restoring trust in its work with the midterms almost here. Jared explores how this incident and a previous one are undermining the industry at a critical time.

Insiders can read more here about what happened with Wedgewood Polling and its implications.

Russia will send its first shipment of diesel to the U.S. today following the president’s deal to import the fuel to address high energy costs. Russian media reported it will carry 40,000 metric tons of fuel . The deal has stirred bipartisan backlash from critics who say it’s giving a boost to the Kremlin in its war against Ukraine.

Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) said she will have to move out of her apartment in Washington, D.C., because of threats she’s received following federal agents’ execution of a search warrant at her residence last week. Omar is apparently under investigation as part of an immigration fraud probe, which she has denounced as baseless.

The White House Correspondents’ Association condemned the White House’s decision to restrict a journalist’s access to cover the president after Trump lashed out at him in the Oval Office. Andrew Feinberg, a correspondent for The Independent, had been scheduled to serve as the print pool reporter today, but he said the White House pulled him from this duty.

SOUTHERN DISCOMFORT : The president has added a stop in Mississippi to his end-of-midterm-cycle blitz, planning a visit just over a week before Election Day.

The Republican National Committee announced the visit on Wednesday. Trump will rally for Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.), who is seeking to fend off a serious challenge from Democrat Scott Colom .

The race is still considered a longshot to flip even in the event of a blue wave, but the decision to add Mississippi to Trump’s tour is notable given the state’s solid red status. A few election handicappers have moved their ratings of the race from “solid” or “safe” Republican to “likely Republican” recently.

The announcement came as Trump held a rally in another deep red state with a surprisingly competitive Senate race: South Carolina.

Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), the sister of Trump’s longtime ally the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), is favored to win reelection, but forecasters are increasingly uncertain as Election Day approaches.

Decision Desk HQ rates Graham’s race against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews as “lean” Republican.

▪ The Hill : Ralph Norman: ‘My family is not going to vote for Darline Graham.’

▪ The Hill : Where prices stand as midterms approach.

RARE LOSS: The Supreme Court temporarily barred the Trump administration from enforcing a policy that would deny gender transition care to federal prisoners, leaving in place a lower-court block over the dissents of conservative justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito.

The brief order did not detail the legal reasoning to temporarily leave in place the block on the policy, which would halt surgeries, taper off hormones for inmates currently receiving them and stop providing social accommodations like makeup, wigs and hair-removal devices.

The decision marks a rare blow for the Trump administration, which has won more than two dozen times when asking the high court to provide emergency relief when a lower court blocked part of Trump’s agenda.

The Supreme Court has allowed other policies for transgender people to remain in place for now, including the administration’s ban on openly transgender troops serving in the military.

▪ The Hill : Olympian asks DOJ watchdog to reconsider probe of Reflecting Pool case.

▪ The Hill : Elena Kagan says court rulings have heightened polarization.

VANCE DEFENDS RAMASWAMY: Vice President Vance criticized some fellow Republicans for their response to Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy ’s (R) controversial attack ad that featured the estranged mother of his Democrat opponent, Amy Acton , discouraging voters from supporting her daughter’s candidacy.

“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” the vice president said at a fraud task force press conference.

Vance, a former Ohio senator, defended the Republican candidate at a rally later in the day, saying, “Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar.”

Acton’s campaign responded to the ad Tuesday evening, noting the candidate has not seen her mother since she was 12 years old, when her mother lost custody of her children after siding with their stepfather, her husband, when he was indicted for raping Acton as a child.

▪ The Hill : Trump to make third visit to Ohio this month for rally.

▪ The Hill : Ohio Sen. Jon Husted (R): ‘I would not have run’ Ramaswamy ad.

CANDIDATE DETAINED: New York congressional candidate Brad Lander (D) was detained by Israeli forces after joining Palestinian farmers at the annual olive harvest in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Wednesday. He was released hours later “after it became known that he was a congressional candidate,” according to Israeli police.

Lander was reportedly one of 90 volunteers who were detained.

The Israeli military said farmers and volunteers did not seek approval for the harvest and were detained because of “the security risk posed by conducting an uncoordinated harvest near an Israeli community,” adding, “ The arrival of dozens of activists as an act intended solely to provoke, which undermines the harvesting process.”

Lander — one of three left-leaning candidates to win primaries in New York City this year with support from Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) — condemned the Israeli occupation as “a crime under international law,” following his detainment, adding, “Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”

▪ Reuters : Israeli elections may change its leader, not Iran war policy.

BRINGING THE HAMMER DOWN : A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found it liable for misleading users about its privacy and content policies.

New Mexico was one of just two states that didn’t join the 48-state settlement with the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. Jurors in the state found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of its consumer protection laws when the British consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested data from Facebook users for political ads during the 2016 election.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez (D) called the ruling “one of the single largest — if not the largest — single state verdict against the company in American history.” Torrez said following an expected appeals process, the money will be put toward public education in the state.

▪ The Hill : New Mexico sues Jeffrey Epstein attorney, accountant.

The president will receive an intelligence briefing at 11 a.m. He will participate in signing time at 3 p.m. He will travel to Sioux City, Iowa, to deliver remarks at 7:30 p.m. EDT and then return to the White House.

The Senate will meet at 9 a.m. for a pro forma session.

The House will convene at 3 p.m. for a pro forma session.

‘HUMANITARIAN’ BACKLASH: U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff is facing backlash from lawmakers for calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” for agreeing to release Stephen Hubbard , an American teacher accused of being a Ukrainian mercenary, after more than four years in Russian custody.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff said to Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.”

The remarks were immediately met with disdain from members of Congress, including from members of the president’s own party, who pointed out Putin’s record of worsening or creating humanitarian crises.

“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) wrote on social platform X, responding to Witkoff’s comments.

“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” he continued. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) responded, “No. Putin is stone cold killer,” while Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) called it “ another embarrassment.”

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), who served more than two decades in the military, responded: “Vladimir Putin is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian. His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life.”

“Appeasement won’t end this war. Pressure will,” she added.

GET OUT : The State Department on Wednesday ordered nonemergency U.S. government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, warning of the possibility of escalated attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis in the country.

“As the Department has repeatedly emphasized, the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area,” a State Department spokesperson told The Hill in a statement.

“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them as they return to the U.S.,” the spokesperson added.

An earlier Reuters report indicated the U.S. government was preparing to order the departure of some personnel and family members from U.S. embassies across the Gulf, but a State Department spokesperson said the report was “inaccurate.”

NBC News reported the U.S. was scaling back its troop presence at military bases in the Middle East and had ordered staff reductions at “multiple diplomatic posts in the region.”

“I don’t know that they are. You are telling me something — I wouldn’t know that,” Trump said when asked about the reports.

The Houthis have been engaged in a war against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and have been attacking infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia as well, including civilian airports and other sites that have led to civilian casualties.

Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said two people were killed and two were injured by falling debris after the country’s air defense intercepted a drone that was targeting Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield yesterday.

articles.title: Can Vance make Trump’s party his own? He should look to Italy’s Giorgia Meloni.
articles.summary: Trump, like Silvio Berlusconi, will be a hard act to follow.
articles.body:
The 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution prevents presidents from being elected to more than two terms. With President Trump winning re-election in 2024, he will not be eligible to run again.

This reality has both Democrats and Republicans asking themselves whether “Trumpism” will survive once he exits the political stage. The second question often debated is who will inherit Trump’s base, and can his successor sustain Trump’s hold on the Republican Party and the MAGA movement.

The person most likely to inherit Trump’s base is Vice President JD Vance. In many ways, Vance is more aligned with the MAGA movement than Trump himself — most notably on foreign policy, U.S. relations with Israel and the role of religion in our nation’s public affairs.

After the assassination of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk in September of 2025, it was Vance who took the leading role in eulogizing Kirk, both defining and defending his Christian populist narrative before the country.

During his tenure in office, Vance has worked hard to develop and maintain close working relationships with a network of MAGA associated advocacy organizations, think tanks, influencers, podcasters, and donors. He is also one of the few high-profile Republican elected officials who has refused to publicly condemn or disavow his friendship with Tucker Carlson, a MAGA favorite who continues to make incendiary remarks about Israel and American Jews.

Although Vance shares Trump’s policy prescriptions on illegal immigration, trade, tariffs, and other domestic issues, he seems far more skeptical of long-standing U.S. global security relationships. He often criticizes NATO and has expressed little public support for defending Taiwan from a potential Chinese invasion.

He has also recently begun to distance himself from Trump on Israel and the war in Iran, and he has been a consistent critic within the administration of U.S. involvement in Ukraine. In fact, Vance has shown little interest, unlike Trump, in using U.S. military power and diplomacy to negotiate peace deals in Gaza, Ukraine, and in the Persian Gulf.

A conservative Catholic convert, Vance is also more likely than Trump to assertively expand religious liberty protections and be more receptive to pro-Life advocates within the Republican Party, which Trump has kept at a distance since his first term in office. The central question is whether Vance can inherit the MAGA movement by modifying its policy interests and direction — or whether Trumpism is impossible to maintain and grow without Trump’s own super-sized personality.

To answer that question, Vance should examine how another gifted populist politician in a Western democracy was able not only to inherit a political movement from a larger-than-life politician, but to transform that movement by making it her own.

At 31 years old, Giorgia Meloni became the youngest minister in the Italian government of the late Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, a billionaire businessman who created and led the conservative Forza Italia Party.

Berlusconi’s personality and politics dominated Italian life between 1994 and 2011, when he served three stints as prime minister. His massive ego and unconventional methods of governing made him a hero to the Italian right and a villain to the left, dividing the country more than any other modern Italian politician. He was Trump before Trump.

After the fall of Berlusconi, Meloni knew that she could not duplicate his cult of personality. She quickly recognized that the conservative movement needed both to change and to be rebranded for her to succeed.

After leaving her mentor Berlusconi and the conservative People of Freedom Party in 2012, Meloni co-founded the populist Brothers of Italy Party. Ten years later, Meloni was elected prime minister.

She quickly adopted a common-sense governing style to forever separate herself from the Berlusconi’s ego-fueled and larger-than-life personality. She did this while embracing a populist policy agenda which included an end to open immigration, less intervention in foreign conflicts, free-speech legal protections, and rejection of a more intrusive EU bureaucracy. She also began to publicly defend traditional marriage, the role of the Catholic Church in public affairs, and Italy’s national sovereignty.

Berlusconi and other right-wing parties had often ignored these cultural issues, preferring to focus on their free-market economic agenda. Meloni’s innovation was to skillfully transform the Italian right from Berlusconi’s transactional politics to a populist movement defined by policy rather than personality.

The biggest problem confronting Meloni was that she could never dominate the news cycle or manipulate the political conversation through the force of her personality the way Berlusconi did. Meloni solved this problem by marrying her straightforward, no-nonsense governing style to a populist policy agenda that embraced many of Berlusconi’s economic and anti-immigration positions, while adding a broader religious and cultural narrative to her politics, to appeal directly to Italian national pride. The strategy has worked brilliantly, uniting the right and making Meloni one of the most popular and influential prime ministers in modern Italian history.

Vance is similarly situated to Meloni in many ways. And to replicate her success, he will need to do something like what she has done. Trump’s larger-than-life personality, unconventional politics and transactional style of governing closely mimics Berlusconi’s long tenure. And Trump, like Berlusconi, will be a hard act to follow.

However, Vance and Meloni have a great deal in common. They both share a direct and straightforward governing style. They also embrace a similar populist policy agenda that focuses on stopping illegal immigration, a healthy mistrust of “free trade” and global institutions, a reluctance to get involved in foreign wars, a skepticism of EU security and economic policies, and a foundational belief that preserving Western civilization and national sovereignty are important goals for both countries.

Will Vance enjoy the same post-Trump success as Meloni has after inheriting and reshaping the Italian right in the post-Berlusconi era? Trump and the MAGA movement seem willing to give Vance that opportunity. Recent polls suggest that he is the leading candidate for the Republican Presidential nomination in 2028, well ahead of current Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who shares Trump’s more aggressive foreign policy agenda.

Vance’s success or failure will be determined by his own political skills and the electorate’s mood at the end of Trump’s term. But the electoral blueprint for successfully following a larger-than-life leader has already been laid out for him by Meloni.

Frank DiFulvio is a professional writer and independent journalist who lives and works in Italy and in Northern Virginia.

articles.title: Rep. Keith Self targeted in alleged assassination plot by Texas teen: report
articles.summary: The 17-year-old suspect allegedly acquired a firearm and planned to target Rep. Keith Self at an event while plotting a separate ISIS attack.
articles.body: Federal authorities arrested a 17-year-old Texas boy accused of plotting to assassinate Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, and carry out a separate terrorist attack in North Texas on behalf of ISIS, according to a local report. The teenager, who has not been publicly identified, was arrested on Oct. 5 after acquiring a firearm, according to federal law enforcement sources cited by WFAA. "I am grateful to the FBI and law enforcement for stopping this threat," Self said in a statement posted on X. "My family and I are safe, and I remain focused on serving the people of Texasâ 3rd District," he continued. "Preserving our constitutional republic from radical Islam means accepting the costs that come with itâname-calling, threats, and worse." MALL OF AMERICA TERROR PLOT THWARTED; SUSPECTED ISIS SYMPATHIZER ARRESTED, FBI ANNOUNCES "Our Founders believed this country was worth the sacrifice," Self added. "I served 25 years in the military because defending freedom was worth the sacrifice. This only strengthens my resolve. I will not back down." Self spoke about the situation to CBS News Texas following the arrest. "When we knew about it, they had him," Self said, admitting he had limited knowledge of what went on. "The FBI, through the Capitol Police, only tells us so much," he told CBS, although he did note, "I understand that they've known about this kid for a while." According to WFAA, the teenager allegedly planned to target Self at an event last Saturday. Federal investigators also believe the suspect was planning a separate attack on behalf of ISIS, the outlet reported. When asked by WFAA whether his public positions on Islamic extremism might explain why he was targeted, Self said he could not be certain. articles.title: Trump llamó a Google para cambiar el nombre del Atlántico y ponerle su apellido: "Lo llamaremos Océano Trump"
articles.standfirst: El presidente asegura que el CEO de Google rechazó la petición
articles.summary: El presidente asegura que el CEO de Google rechazó la petición
articles.body: Después del Golfo de América, Donald Trump ha puesto la vista en un objetivo mucho más grande. El presidente de Estados Unidos ha contado ante sus seguidores que intentó cambiar el nombre de uno de los grandes océanos del planeta, y que la respuesta que recibió no fue la que esperaba. Durante un mitin, Trump relató que se puso en contacto con Google para pedir que Google Maps rebautizara el océano Atlántico como “Océano Trump”. Según su versión, habló con el consejero delegado de la compañía, Sundar Pichai, a quien planteó directamente la propuesta. Pero esta vez la respuesta fue negativa. Trump explicó que la compañía le dijo que los océanos son diferentes porque abarcan muchos países. Al reproducir la contestación que recibió, el mandatario la resumió así: “Por favor, no nos pida que hagamos eso”. El presidente aseguró que dejará pasar la negativa y que el Atlántico seguirá llamándose así. Aunque aclaró que se trataba de una broma, también reconoció que, pensándolo mejor, le parecía que “no era una mala idea”. Además, deslizó otras opciones, como llamar “Océano Trump” al Pacífico o recurrir al nombre de “Océano de las Américas”. No es la primera vez que Trump impulsa un cambio de nombre geográfico. Al comienzo de su segundo mandato firmó una orden ejecutiva para rebautizar el Golfo de México como Golfo de América, y en aquella ocasión Google Maps sí aplicó el cambio para los usuarios de Estados Unidos. El mandatario sostiene que entonces bastó una llamada para que la empresa aceptara, e incluso asegura que le dijeron que era “una gran idea”. También presume del éxito comercial del nuevo nombre, como la venta de gorras del Golfo de América. Google ya ha explicado en otras ocasiones que los nombres geográficos de su plataforma se basan en fuentes oficiales y que aplica políticas específicas para los lugares cuya denominación varía entre países.

articles.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton clashed over Trump, transgender athletes and AI in a heated Kansas Senate debate on Wednesday.
articles.body: Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night. The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall â a topic touched on during the debate. Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate. SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Debate opens with candidates confronted over personal controversies The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates. Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. "Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric." Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse. Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation. FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS "I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part." Marshall says 'President Trump is not always right' Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week. "And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd. Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda. "No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump. Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports. "Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right." Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate. Both candidates say there are 'two genders' The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are. "There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls." "There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded. TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports. Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females. "I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight." Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology." Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people. Hamilton calls AI an 'existential threat' â but can't name regulations he'd support Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons. "We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said. But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer. "You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers. Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement. Hamilton pushed back sharply. "This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best." BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH Hamilton calls Biden's border policies a 'disaster' Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle." The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed. "The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders." "I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."
